Mr. Chairman, I rise to address myself to the question I posed earlier today, regarding a situation which I earnestly request the Minister of Labour to look at with more realism than he has done up to now. I refer to the strike in the trucking industry in the province of Ontario which, as was indicated earlier, has been going on now for some nine weeks with disastrous results to some 8,000 families, because there are 8,500 truckers involved. I imagine this has also had serious results for the 55 trucking firms involved, as well as for many hundreds of shippers throughout the province.
I appreciate that negotiations have been taking place for a long time, and that there was a conciliation procedure which was followed through the co-operation of both the federal and provincial governments. There
March 25, 1968

was a conciliation board report which the unions were not willing to accept.
I want to draw your attention first, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that I am not raising this matter on the floor of the federal House of Commons lightly. I know a little about the organization of this industry, having been involved in court in one or two cases on problems of jurisdiction as between federal and provincial authorities. I am certain in my own mind that the strike involves the federal authority very much more than it involves the provincial one because, in my opinion, at least 70 per cent of the employees concerned are engaged in interprovincial and international transportation and are therefore covered by the federal law.
Last Saturday night I was in Hamilton, and that is the reason I am raising this issue with some urgency today. I addressed a meeting concerned with raising some funds to augment the benefits paid to striking workers who are members of local 879 of the teamsters' union which has its headquarters in that city. I learned from some of the workers that they are reaching the point now where their personal lives and the lives of their families are pretty seriously affected by the continuation of the strike.
I also learned from the president of the local union, Mr. Ray Taggart, who is also chairman of the negotiating committee involving all the unions concerned, that there are now three remaining issues of any importance in dispute between the unions and the trucking firms. The first is the question of a 40 hour week; the second is the question of the owner-operators, and the third is the question of certain retaliatory steps taken by some firms against local unions for earlier alleged wildcat strikes.
From my knowledge of the situation I would urge the Minister of Labour not to worry about what are called reprisals; that is, the actions by trucking firms, grievances and damages against local unions, particularly the local in Hamilton; because I am confident that cannot and will not be an obstacle to a settlement if the 40 hour week problem is settled. That is why I speak with very considerable indignation about the attitude of the Minister of Labour in a situation of this sort.
I have often said that a strike is a very regrettable interruption of the normal peaceful labour-management relations that in most cases does, and in all cases should, if at all possible, obtain. When a strike does occur it usually occurs as a result of the accumulation
Interim Supply
of pretty serious grievances by the people concerned. When a government has the power to do something that will hasten the settlement of a strike but fails to act, it is guilty of a very reprehensible omission of action within its authority. If a government cannot do anything because the matter is merely one of negotiation between the workers and the management concerned, and only offers its good offices and the offices of its labour department to seek conciliation, mediation and negotiation, that is one thing. But when a government has within its hands a law for which it is responsible but fails to act quickly enough or with enough vigour and devotion to the situation, then it is dangerously dilatory.
This government does have a law which it brought in and which was heralded throughout the country as a great social advance for labour, and it could act. The previous minister of labour, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare, made some very moving speeches about this great benefit he was producing for the workers under federal jurisdiction when he introduced the Canada Labour (Standards) Code.
There were some wonderful advertisements in the papers.

There were some very good ads in the papers, as my leader suggests. I did not have the pleasure of listening to the minister when he introduced this legislation, because I was not a member of parliament at the time; but because of my interest in this field I carefully read the reports of his speeches which indicated that they were speeches of great hope and satisfaction, if not smugness, in regard to the great good he was performing for the workers of Canada.
[DOT] (12:00 noon)
So you pass a law, and the law says that the standard work week is to be 40 hours. Then you have a strike of workers precisely on the issue of the 40 hour week, and the Minister of Labour sits back and lets the strike continue for nine weeks, doing nothing at all about it.
Shame.

I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that I might have raised this issue on the floor many weeks ago. I did not. Instead I wrote to the Minister of Labour as long ago as February 22. I was not interested then, no more than I am interested now, in raising the issue on the floor merely to make a lot of noise. So I wrote to the Minister of Labour

March 25, 1966
Interim Supply
on February 22 and pleaded with him to make a decision and announce the decision on the application for deferment of the hours of work provided under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code.
I indicated in my letter to him that even if he was not prepared to say the 40 hour week shall be applied immediately, he would perform a service in the present strike if he had the imagination and the will and were ready to say at least that the hours of work from then on would be 42 or 43 hours a week for the next 18 months, and at the end of that time we would have to go back to what the law provides. Even that would have been of some help to the negotiating parties.
I received an answer from the minister dated February 28. I will paraphrase it instead of reading it-and I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I will paraphrase it accurately-in which he said, "The parties are negotiating. Therefore I am not going to make any statement. I do not think it would serve any purpose."
Therefore I wrote again to the minister on March 1 and pointed out to him what was obvious, that it is his law; that he has a duty to administer it; that he has a duty to make sure the law is applied, not at the whim of employers or even of unions but in the interests of the public; that he has a duty so to act without waiting for the negotiations to drag on and allowing all the evils of the strike to continue. He replied saying, "I don't agree with you. I am not going to act because these people are in negotiation."
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Before the strike took place, how many hours a week were these people working in the transport industry in Ontario?

An outrageous number of hours, in my opinion. Many of them were working as many as 48 hours a week. Some of them were working a lesser number of hours, but many were working as many as 48 hours a week. They have been fighting to my knowledge for many years to have their hours reduced to the 40 hours which is the standard work week throughout Canada.
Not only has parliament said that there was to be a 40 hour week, and this is what I consider to be-I use this word deliberately-the criminality of the Minister of Labour in not taking action, but I am confident in my

mind that the union might not even have asked for the 40 hour week if it had not been the law. It is an experienced, well established union, and might have asked for a reduction only of four or five hours from the 48 rather than a reduction of the full eight hours. The only reason it asked for the 40 hour week is that it said "Here is the law of Canada. Our parliament said to us that we should not work more than a standard work week of 40 hours. So we go to the negotiating table and ask for it. We ask for what the law provides. Then we are denied it, not only by the trucking firms but by the government that introduced this law." I am almost speechless with indignation at this kind of irresponsible and callous behaviour toward a law of parliament for which the government itself is responsible.
1 said the other day in another connection that I took the trouble, at some considerable time and with some help, to go through the various Canada Gazettes some time ago to find out how many firms and what firms asked for deferment, particularly of part 1 of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, namely the part that deals with hours of work. This was because a question placed on the order paper by my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North had not been answered, and I do not think it has yet been answered. Therefore I looked for this information myself. I think I am not exaggerating, in fact I am sure I am not, when I say there is not a single firm that comes under federal jurisdiction which has not asked for deferment under part 1 of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code.
May I take a moment to remind hon. members of the following facts about that code. The code provides that if an application for deferment is made and it appeared in the Canada Gazette for July 1, 1965, there was an automatic deferment of part 1 of the act without any other action by anybody. That automatic deferment could last for no more than 18 months; then the minister is given authority to provide for a further deferment for another 18 months once he has made up his mind on the application for deferment. After that there is provision for a further inquiry in case there is another application for deferment. This, after all, makes the act not a very demanding piece of legislation, despite what the minister boasted about in regard to its provisions. It was not providing
March 25. 1966

the 40 hour week for employees under federal jurisdiction; it was providing an opportunity for them to get it in 36 months or perhaps a little longer.
This is what my letters to the minister requested him to do, namely to indicate that they would have it at the end of the period of deferment provided in the act. Even that the minister has refused to do. If members are told by anybody who replies, if anybody does reply for the government, that there are other issues, let me say that after long years of experience in negotiations and many conversations with leaders of the negotiating committee of the union in the past couple of months, I am absolutely certain that if the minister had the will to carry into effect the law which his government put on the books, there would be a settlement of this strike within days after his so doing; because the issue about which the membership feels most keenly, and rightly so, is that of the 40 hour week.
When I spoke to a number of these workers last Saturday night in Hamilton the answer invariably was "All the people in the Steel Company of Canada, in Canadian Westinghouse and in every other industry in Hamilton, and the same in Windsor, London and Toronto, work a 40 hour week. This is the standard. The federal parliament passed a law giving us the right to the 40 hour work week. Why don't we get it? And we are 'so-and-so' if we go back to work before we get it."
The members of the negotiating committee have said to me-and I am sure they would not mind my saying it to this House of Commons, even though it is part of their negotiations-that they will not necessarily insist on getting the 40 hour week the moment the agreement is signed; that they are prepared to consider-this is why the earlier motion I moved did not say "the immediate implementation of the 40 hour week" but a "rapid transition" toward it-a rapid transition toward the 40 hour week if the employers were willing to consider it.
I have outlined the facts of this matter, Mr. Chairman. I do not intend to prolong my speech. I say it is in the hands of this government to take steps today which within a week will settle the strike which has now lasted for nine weeks. I say that the government has a duty under its own law to take those steps today, not next month or two months from now after people have suffered unnecessarily for a further eight to nine

weeks. The government has a duty to do this today, because the law is there on the statute books. I say if it does that, it will act like a government with conscience and sense of responsibility for the laws of Canada. If it does not, it will show complete callousness and complete contempt for its own law and its duties under that law.

the employers too hard, in their opinion, this is what they have done. In the letter of February 22 to the Minister of Labour, to which I have referred, I said this, Mr. Chairman:

A mere announcement by him that he is giving favourable consideration to that, and that this session or within a short time the act will be amended to cover this loophole, would be sufficient for the unions to give careful consideration to withdrawing their demands in the present negotiations.
These are the reasons, Mr. Chairman, I considered the question one of urgent importance, and why I raised it on the floor of this house. In my submission it is entirely within the hands of this government to end the trucking strike within a few days if the government will act.

I think we all share that concern. Perhaps the solution is not quite as simple as the hon. member has suggested. I wish it were that simple.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is in the house, will recall that when the labour code was under discussion in

the house grave concern was expressed about the effect it would have on the trucking industry because their operations were based on a longer work period. There was also a suggestion that the workers in the trucking industry were not primarily the employees the code was designed to affect. They were not the workers we wanted to upgrade. The workers with whom we were concerned at that time were those receiving ridiculously low wages or ridiculously low hourly rates. The code, which was widespread in application, had to include workers in industries who had collective agreements, and workers who had bargaining agents who had great experience in this labour relations field.
The hon. member for York South refers to the fact that the law sets up a 40 hour week and asks why we are not applying this law to the trucking industry. I wish it were that simple. In so far as certain industries are concerned, such as this one, where serious dislocation would be created by the application of the law, there is a provision for deferment. One of the reasons for deferment is the fact that in rtiany cases unions in these industries have bargained for benefits far beyond those provided under this minimal standards legislation. We did not want to dislocate them too greatly.
Great concern on this point was expressed at that time by N.D.P. members as well as by Liberals and, I believe, members of the official opposition, although I do not have the record before me at the moment. It was felt that if we applied the 40 hour week to these employees without a sufficient interval of time for this arrangement to be worked out between employees, employers and the government, serious loss of wages would result.
I can recall this concern being expressed in this house at the time the code was being discussed. This is one of the reasons this procedure for deferment was provided in the legislation. We all recall that the trucking industry put on a tremendous lobby to have their industry exempted entirely from the legislation. This pressure was resisted, but at the same time there was great concern on the part of employees in the transportation industry that this 40 hour week provision would be applied without any qualification, and too quickly. It was for this reason the deferment period was provided. This was especially true where serious dislocation would be experienced, and wide latitude was given for negotiation between employers and employees.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise a question arising from the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat. The concern some of us had about these deferment provisions was that the government, with these provisions in the code, would do precisely what apparently it is now doing, namely making the real purposes of the act completely inoperative.
That is the concern which was in the minds of those in this party who were in this house when that code was put through. I myself very clearly remember attempting to suggest that the principle of the 40 hour week was the one which would be applied. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre reminds me that we made specific proposals for cutting down the deferment period.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: My point, which I thought I had made clear, was that there was, of course, concern on all sides of the house. There was concern on this side and in the New Democratic party that any succeeding government might in fact use this legislation to deny the privileges of the act to those employees that it was most desirous they should reach, namely those who were employed earning less than the minimal wage standards. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments in connection with the remarks of the hon. member for York South. I regret that he has left the

house, but I am sure he has left for a good reason.
The Canada Labour (Standards) Code is made up of four components; hours of work, wages, statutory holidays and vacations with pay. Before I get into the provisions of the code may I say it is still the fact that this legislation, providing as it does for a range of conditions in these four fields, has no rival in any country of the world. It is unrivalled in its comprehensiveness and in the extent to which it attempts to apply favourable conditions to the life of the worker.
With respect to statutory holidays there were no deferment provisions. With respect to vacations with pay there were no deferment provisions. Deferment provisions were provided in the case of minimum wages and hours of work. There have been requests to defer the application of the minimum wage but none of these requests has been granted. That fact has not been noted. At least to my knowledge there has been no request granted to defer application of the minimum wage.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
With respect to hours of work, two choices were available to the government at that time. One choice was to do what had been done in almost every other jurisdiction, which was to provide for a range of exemptions so the law would never be operative with respect to hours of work. That was the course taken in the United States; it was the course taken in the province of Saskatchewan; it was the course taken in almost every province of Canada where, with respect to hours of work, there were a series of blanket escape clauses so the hours of work would never become applicable.
We resisted that course and provided that within a certain period of time the standard hours, or the 40 hour week, would become applicable. I remember very clearly the pressures that came upon me as Minister of Labour not to maintain that principle, from the trucking industry, from the employers and from the employees in the trucking industry. I had delegations of workers coming to my office asking that this provision not go into effect because they were afraid, as we all were, that the immediate application of the 40 hour week would result in a reduction in take home pay unless there was a supplementary provision proviidng for the maintenance of take home pay, as it had been made available under the previous regime.
March 25, 1966

We knew the effects of that. It would be very disruptive, especially because our jurisdiction federally is applicable to interprovincial and international trucking, and there were many trucking firms under our jurisdiction which were in competition with trucking firms that were totally within provincial jurisdiction. Provincial ministers of labour and provincial governments were very concerned about the effect of the immediate application of our law with respect to firms that were not within our jurisdiction, and which would be immediately affected.
We took the course that there would be an 18 month provision for deferment upon application, and then, if in the opinion of the minister it were necessary, an inquiry would be held and a further order made in order to determine what ought to be the appropriate regime with respect to hours in any industry.
The trucking industry, of course, provides a classic case. Hon. gentlemen on the other side are complaining today about the effects of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. I am surprised, because the evidence of the bite, of the effect, of the importance of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code is demonstrated in what is happening in the trucking industry today. In the absence of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code this problem would not arise, and there would be a continued regime of longer hours prevailing in an industry which ought to have reduced its hours a long time ago. In the absence of that code this reduction would not have been effected.
Of course there is disruption. Does the hon. member for York South think social development and social progress will take place without some disruption in normal patterns of counduct and normal patterns of behaviour? If he does, it seems to me he is escaping from his own position as a member in this house.
That is the situation. Undoubtedly, by the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, the government and parliament have tilted the balance in favour of reduced hours. We have left the matter to be worked out, if possible, within the framework of collective bargaining, with the sure knowledge that there is an opportunity within the law, through determined or predetermined procedures by parliament, to induce an appropriate regime of lower hours in this industry.
I am surprised that the hon. member for York South should take this occasion to beat the government over the head with the

Canada Labour (Standards) Code, especially when we all know that at the present time very serious negotiations are taking place. Provincial and federal officials are at work in Toronto and other centres in Ontario in order to induce a settlement. Active discussions are taking place in Toronto now, and will take place over this week end, among Ontario departmental officials, federal departmental officials, and representatives of the trucking industry on the employer and on the employee side. They are considering further proposals, and the Ontario department involved is hopeful for a settlement. The federal department involved is also hopeful for a settlement.
I do not think I should add anything further that might frustrate the achievement of this settlement, except that I was persuaded to say something by the remarks of the hon. member for York South who, I think, unfairly used the Canada Labour (Standards) Code to denounce the government for appropriate action being taken at the present time.
This is a good labour bill. The hon. gentleman did nothing to help it by his conduct and his remarks today.

If the minister thinks just two members from Cape Breton island are going to give him difficulty, I want to warn him now that he has another think coming, because there are ten members from Nova Scotia sitting here in the Progressive Conservative party who are going to create for him a lot more trouble than he has had yet, if he does not smarten up.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Minster of National Health and Welfare that if matters

involving Nova Scotia and involving $12 million are to be made public, those announcements should be made in the proper atmosphere. They should be made in an atmosphere which indicates that some weight is given to the announcement that is to be made, an atmosphere which indicates that some importance is attached to the programs to be carried out, and some attention paid to the problems we have in Nova Scotia. No attempt should be made to smuggle these announcements into the House of Commons, through colleagues of the minister, in a clandestine way because members opposite are fearful that some member of the Progressive Conservative party might, in some strange way, get credit for what has been done. It is not a matter of who gets credit for what; it is a matter of keeping federal-provincial relations at a high level.
When we were in office no federal minister was complaining about the kind of treatment he was receiving. No federal minister was complaining about the way the premier of Nova Scotia was doing things. There was co-operation.
I see that our great and true friend, the leading spokesman for the Atlantic provinces, has joined the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Perhaps he will be good enough to rise in this debate and tell the people of Nova Scotia in a straightforward way what the Atlantic Development Board is trying to do, instead of smuggling the announcement into the house in a clandestine manner with the help of the hon. member for St. John's West. Let us have no more of the type of federal-provincial relationship which has been in existence in the past. We are sick of that in Nova Scotia. If this government think they are given rough times by the members of the Progressive Conservative party from Nova Scotia, they have no idea of what is coming.
I will be glad to reply to the hon. gentleman.
Why don't you do it in the proper way?
The hon. member is, of course, an authority on proper conduct.
I am just as much an authority on it as you are.

I do not pretend to be. I try to keep my own conscience and I find that quite a large enough task. I do not try to
March 25, 1966

keep other men's consciences, and I think we would have a much better parliament if other members took this attitude.
Hear, hear.

There seems to be a notion, one which has not always existed in this parliament, that no private member on this side of the house has any rights. It is also a rule of this house that one cannot reflect on the motives of other members. The hon. member for St. John's West, even though he supports the government, has just as much right to ask a question in this house as has the hon. member for Cumberland. He asked a question, as was his right. The question did not appear to the Speaker to be of a kind which should be answered on orders of the day. On the other hand the hon. member for Cape Breton South asked a question and I was permitted to answer very briefly.
I am very pleased to have the opportunity now to expand on my earlier answer. I am very pleased that the premier of Nova Scotia made this application to the Atlantic Development Board for a new kind of aid. It is true that in the case of Mactaquac and Baie d'Espoir grants were made to assist in the development of hydroelectric power. At that time the government of Nova Scotia took the view that it had no hydroelectric resources which it wished to develop. This was not the kind of government aid the premier of Nova Scotia wanted.
The premier and I had quite lengthy discussions, and the chairman of the board had many more discussions with the premier of Nova Scotia about aid to secondary industries. A good deal has been done in this field, but in the main this kind of activity is taken care of by the area development agency of the Department of Industry. The premier recognized this very well. Though the board had set aside $20 million at the request of Nova Scotia to be reserved for this kind of aid, after the area development agency was established and after certain provisions were made for industrial parks and things of that kind, the premier made this submission to the board which I welcome very much, because it is in accord with what I had suggested when I was on the other side of the house.
It was my view that more coal should be used in Nova Scotia for the development of electric power in that province to promote industrial growth. This proposition was made by the board to the government, and the
Interim Supply
government gave it the most careful consideration. We came to the conclusion-and we only reached this conclusion yesterday-that in principle this was a very sound thing to do. The Atlantic Development Board is having a meeting in Halifax on Monday, at which time the development of this program will be further considered. There will be discussion, I am sure, between officials of the board and, probably, the chairman of the board and the government of Nova Scotia to achieve an end which I am sure the hon. member for Cumberland has very much at heart, that is the accomplishment of anything we can possibly do to provide an infrastructure and base for greater industrial growth in the Atlantic provinces. It has been a matter of deep regret to me-and I am sure the hon. member will not question me when I say this-that we had not until yesterday been able to find projects in Nova Scotia of the kind that come within the scope of the board on a scale comparable with those in New Brunswick and Newfoundland.
This was only because of the electrical development. As far as other things are concerned there is not much disparity among the three large Atlantic provinces. But these grants of $20 million for hydro development did make the distribution look very unequal. I did not like this any more than the hon. gentleman did, but I also respected the basic principles upon which the board has acted, that we must co-operate with the provinces concerned.
This represents an important proposal for the improvement of the infrastructure of Nova Scotia. It will also do something I have wanted to see done for a long time. I believe that if we can transform the coal in Nova Scotia in such a way that it can be used as electricity in Nova Scotia, or even elsewhere in the Atlantic provinces, as a base for better industrial development there it will be a lot better than paying a big subvention to ship it to Quebec or Ontario. I hope this will be productive of secondary developments which will enable us to go a lot further in this direction.
I go so far as to say I am grateful to the hon. member for Cumberland for raising this matter and giving me an opportunity to say much more than, under the rules, I could possibly have said in answer to a question this morning.

I think it would have been quite easy for me to issue a press release this morning. I agree with the view about executive actions, that where there is no policy involved-and the policy of aid of this kind was established some time ago-and we merely are carrying out a policy, we should do the things we have to do here, such as pass estimates and legislation, and should not be taking up time in the house with self advertising announcements made on motions in the House of Commons.

In my department, which spreads itself around in many directions-some people think too far-I suppose we issue one or two press releases a day. Most of these are as dull as dishwater. If I were to come in and make statements on motions on each of these things I think the hon. member really could criticize my conduct, and perhaps I should be expelled from the house.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to go back to the issue I raised and in respect of which the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the hon. member for Hamilton East spoke. First may I say that the hon. member for Hamilton East said something about political opportunism, and I would like to say with all the kindness I can that that is an unworthy retort made when there is nothing to be said which is worth saying. I would hope that the young, and I am sure well meaning, member for Hamilton East would not quickly descend to that kind of unworthy reply.
Second, Mr. Chairman, I have always thought I am reasonably able to articulate my ideas, but apparently one fails frequently when exchanging ideas with political opponents. I did not speak from notes, but I would be ready to bet whatever reputation I have on the statement that never did I, in my statement today or at any other time, criticize the code. I did not say that the labour code was bad. I did not criticize any part of the act which the minister introduced, today nor at any other time.

What I criticized was the failure of the minister to act in accordance with the code and the circumstances as they require it. That is what I criticized, not the code. I am perfectly well aware that my colleagues who were in parliament when this code was introduced supported it. Any criticism they had was with regard to deferment. So I am aware they support it, and so do I. I do not hesitate for one moment to say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that it is a useful piece of legislation, even though introduced by a political party which I do not support. I was glad to see it on the statute book. I said it then, and I say it now without hesitation.
I say to the hon. member for Hamilton East that it is wrong to suggest I was trying to do something for political opportunism. Let me tell him why. I spoke to the Minister of Labour on a few occasions and said I did not want to ask a question because I did not want to make this a matter of political controversy on the floor of parliament, knowing that negotiations might be taking place. That is not the way to deal with negotiations.
As I said earlier I wrote the minister a letter a month ago without making it public. The hon. member can think what he likes, but I tell him I desisted from making any public statement except to ask an occasional question, as did the hon. member for Ontario, as to how the negotiations were going on, so long as it seemed to me that the negotiations were taking place. The point I wish to make is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare-and I say this with respect-is mistaken when he says serious negotiations have taken place. The fact, as I am instructed by the leader of the union, is that the negotiations have not been serious and that the parties have met and dispersed.
The fact is that the person who now has become the chief conciliation officer in the provincial government, Mr. William Dickie for whom I have the greatest respect and with whom I have worked for many years, has been unable to get the parties to discuss their issues seriously. My entire point was and is that even though a minister has the right to defer, he has a duty to see what the developing situation is and to take action if the developing situation requires it. In my humble opinion it requires it now.
I did not raise this matter in the first two, three, four or five weeks of this strike; I raised it after the strike had been on for nine or ten weeks. If you let this thing alone it can
March 25, 1966

drag on and have permanent consequences to the trucking industry. As shippers develop new, alternative ways of shipping goods, both the firms and the employees will be permanently harmed.
I raised the matter today because I see no possibility of a quick settlement which the situation requires. I have no doubt that if you leave it alone it will be settled in some weeks. I raised it today because this mornings' papers carried the news of the Ontario Federation of Labour coming into the picture, because there was news of the Minister of Labour in Ontario saying in the legislature that there was no use his doing anything about it because the major responsibility is that of the federal minister of labour.
These are the incidents and facts in the matter, and it is my submission that it is the duty of a member of this house who has some knowledge of the affair to raise it today and not next week or the week after. I did use strong language, because it seems to me, in my study of political science, there is nothing more reprehensible than a good law which is not implemented. It raises false hopes; the hopes are then dashed because the administration refuses to use the good law which it has. This is the basis of the complaint.
I do not wish to take any more time of the committee. However, I would like to repeat an appeal to the minister. If he is satisfied from his knowledge that serious negotiations are taking place over the week end, then he will not take any action today or tomorrow. If I may say so, I will know on Monday whether they have been serious; we both will know whether the negotiations have been serious. If it should look as though they are approaching settlement then, sure, leave it alone for another day or two; but if it looks, as I am sure it does, that the normal course will take weeks longer, then I appeal to the minister to use the authority he has under the good law-and I use this term deliberately-in accordance with its terms and thus hasten settlement of this regrettable strike.

[The Chairman.]

During the last session of parliament we passed the Labour (Standards) Code. According to members on the other side the passage of this act would guarantee to all employees coming under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament certain basic minimums such as $1.25 per hour, time and a half for overtime and a 40 hour week. The 40 hour week was so good, that the government of Canada advertised it in a full page advertisement in the newspapers. Hon. members will recall we raised a question about this because the advertisement included a picture of the former minister of labour, but it was alleged this was just a drawing which looked remarkably like him.
Being a curious member of parliament, I put some questions on the order paper which were answered on February 2, 1966. Hon. members can find the questions and answers on page 573 of Hansard. One of the questions I asked was, how much money was spent on an advertising campaign to explain to the

Canadian people the provisions of the Canadian Labour (Standards) Code?
The answer revealed that the total amount spent on advertising was $185,000. I then asked for a breakdown of how the money was spent as between daily newspapers, weeklies, radio and so on. I would not have minded if the Liberal Party had spent its own campaign funds. Would it take a full 18 months? Would it take less than that or would he come back and ask for an extension of that time? There are thousands of people on strike, Mr. Chairman. The whole business of shipping goods in a large part of Ontario is being made extremely difficult owing to the strike. I am not suggesting that the minister proclaim the 40 hour week section right away, though I think he should have done so by now. and the industry on the other side. I think it is a disgrace and negligence of the worst kind that the minister has not only not proclaimed that section of the act but, more than that, has refused to give any indication when he will act in that regard.

I do not know what pressures are being exerted on the Minister of Labour to postpone the implementation of the provisions of the code but I think he should do the job he is required to do by law and either proclaim this section now or announce the date when its provisions will come into effect.

Mr. Chairman, just a few words following the remarks made by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat and also those made at noon by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) about the teamsters who are on strike in Ontario.
Both hon. members concerned urged the government and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) to enforce the section of the federal legislation concerning the 40 hour week.
I asked the hon. member for York South what were the hours of work before the strike.

They varied between 42, 43 and 48 hours a week. What I find strange is that not so long ago, about a week ago or at the beginning of this week, both hon. members protested against the increase in the cost of living and asked that a price control board be set up in Canada to prevent such increases. Today, the government is urged to intervene in that labour conflict which has been going on for nine weeks, so that the regular work week will be reduced to 40 hours and time and a half will be paid after 40 hours.
How can they reconcile their anti-inflation policy in their opposition to increases in the cost of living and their price and salary control policy, on the one hand, and their asking the government to help increase the salaries and income of the workers, in this case truck drivers in the province of Ontario, on the other?
Those people often like, Mr. Chairman, to quote as examples countries like Russia and Czechoslovakia where everyone works, where there is full employment. Well, I went to Russia and Czechoslovakia last year and I found that, after 50 years of communist rule in Russia, the work week was 46 hours and the right to strike did not exist.
When the workers protest against the boss which is the government everywhere, they can be condemned to hang or to other forms of punishment by that same government.
Mr. Chairman, the Ralliement Creditiste is certainly in favour of workers living decently and enjoying better working conditions throughout Canada.
Although this question of labour is primarily one of provincial jurisdiction, Quebec coming under the provincial government of Quebec and Ontario under the provincial government of Ontario, first representations should be made to the provincial authorities and not to the federal. The federal authorities should be called upon last but not with a view to initiating certain steps or recommendations.
The member for York South made another point this morning, to the effect that after nine weeks of strike, they complain that their wives and children are suffering hardships. That is not the fault of truck owners, the Ontario government, nor that of Ottawa. I say and I repeat, that the ones to be blamed are those labour leaders who spend their time rousing employees against the employers. Instead of acting as conciliators between labour and management, they distribute boxing gloves to both groups, so that hatred is
March 25, 1966

Supply-Labour
fostered as much as possible between employers and employees.
If strike promoters in Canada could prove to me that a strike has solved labour problems, then I would fall into step with them. Never, anywhere in the world, has a strike solved any labour problem. Still, labour leaders strive constantly to maintain misunderstanding between management and labour. To what advantage? To whose advantage? For the benefit of people who, as in Russia, have established a government which is the absolute master of all and without whose permission no one can act freely or decide for himself.
Mr. Chairman, many people contended in the past, that I was opposed to trade unions, that I fought them. No. I am all for unions, but I say that blue-collar and white-collar workers, in short all social classes must be represented by a competent union, to speak on their behalf. I am not for certain organizations working against others. No. I favour an organization which serves the best interests of its membership, which assists its membership, which, in short, is a conciliatory organization, not a boxing or wrestling organization. Those class struggles are what we are strongly against, in any province, indeed in Canada.
We also oppose those allegations or those positions adopted by the members of the New Democratic party, who often advocate salary increases and higher standards of living for workers. We agree, but let them try to reach agreement, to submit a logical policy of what they want for the worker, for the Canadian people as a whole.
We cannot, on the one hand, raise the price of goods and, on the other, say that we want to fight inflation, just as we cannot keep on raising salaries, which enter in the cost of operations, of merchandise or consumer goods, without causing inflation or without going around in circles, as I said recently. Mr. Chairman, let those people try to be logical with themselves, in their proposals.
Unions are necessary, but there are union leaders in Canada who are less than necessary, who are even detrimental to understanding in this country, who spend their time stirring the various classes of the population, instead of enlightening them. As a matter of fact, all strikes, without exception, have been detrimental to those who took part in them or supported them. And strikes have been occurring in every sphere of the economic activity of our country.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
In fact, there almost was a strike of Quebec civil servants which was fortunately averted at the last minute. However, this strike will result in higher taxes in the province of Quebec. Because of this increase in taxes, some people-and we too-will cry out against the higher cost of living and the threat of inflation. Why? Because we know that under our present system, it is impossible to find an acceptable solution likely to improve the standard of living of Canadians without increasing the cost of living.
The standard of living of Canadians is being raised today, but immediately or within a few days or a few weeks, the cost of living will be just as high as before. So, nothing has been gained, and we have been going around in circles like this for at least 25 years.
It is funny, Mr. Chairman. While no solution has been found to help our workers, our organizations, our industrialists, in short, the entire population, in the same breath, the government, through the Departments of Public Works, of National Revenue or of Finance, when it is not the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) himself, comes to the assistance of underdeveloped countries.
This morning, I asked the government where will be found the funds required to loan $1,717,000, without interest, to the government of Ceylon in order to help or complete the modernizing of an airport in that country.
We can do it for others, and I wonder why it cannot be done for our country. Why is the government powerless to help the municipalities, the provinces, the school boards of our country, in short, to help the workers, the white collar workers, the Canadians who toil and build this country?
It seems that when we put a question to find out the reason for the government's inaction or why they do not use the Bank of Canada to finance without interest the needs of the provinces and the municipalities, as they do for other countries, it seems that we never have the right to ask these questions.
We can ask questions about the teamsters, about the truck drivers who are not making enough wages, who are working too many hours, but we may not ask questions concerning our financial or monetary system, which is very well operated to help the underdeveloped countries of the world but is not at all suitable to help the Canadian people.
Mr. Chairman, I have no further comments on item le of the labour department, but I

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT Marine services-
5e. Administration, operation and maintenance, $210,000.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to raise an extremely important matter arising from an event which took place in Montreal harbour on September 14 of last year when in the early morning a ship of Canada Steamship Lines, the Fort William, lost her equilibrium-I think that is the proper term-or lost her stability and capsized. As a result there was a movement in the steel which was part of this vessel's cargo. This caused sparks and resulted in an explosion. The ship sank and the lives of five of the seamen aboard the ship were lost. Even though there was a commission of investigation into this tragedy I submit there is a certain guilt devolving upon Canada Steamship Lines and upon the Department of Transport and the government in general in connection with this tragedy.
It may be mere coincidence that for the past two days the house has been talking about murder. The circumstances of the event which took place on September 14 when the Fort William sank were not very far short of murder. Later I will make a few brief quotations from the report of the committee of investigation to indicate the extent of the guilt which I think exists with respect to this tragedy and the loss of the lives of these five sailors.
A court of investigation or committee of inquiry was set up under Mr. Justice H. F. Gibson. Before I read from the report of his findings I should like to make a comment or two about certain general matters which are also applicable to this particular investigation. In the first place, the unlicensed personnel of the ship, that is, the sailors, were not parties to the inquiry. It is true that some of them were called as witnesses but there is a distinction between being a party to an inquiry and simply appearing as a witness. The only parties to this formal investigation were Canada Steamship Lines, the master of the ship, Samuel Wilkinson, and the first, second and third mates.
Since the sailors were not parties to the inquiry they were not entitled to be represented by counsel and they were therefore not permitted the protection which counsel offers or should offer to people who appear before such inquiries. Because they were denied the right to their own counsel they were not able or may not have been able to tell the story of the tragedy from their point 23033-202
Supply-Transport
of view inasmuch as they were limited to answering questions by the commission and by counsel for the parties, namely, Canada Steamship Lines and the officers aboard the Fort William. Yet one of the individuals who appeared as a witness before this inquiry was on watch at the time the tragedy occurred and played an important role in it. This was the situation in the case we are considering and it is the situation with respect to other similar cases where sailors, unlicensed personnel, are denied the right to have counsel represent them at hearings of this kind. I say their rights and freedom are not fully protected.
Similarly, the widows of the five seamen, not being parties to the investigation, were unable to be represented by counsel even though the activities of their late husbands aboard the ship might have been brought into question. I think this is another failure on the part of the laws of Canada and in my opinion such groups should have the right to be parties to investigations of this kind and to be represented by counsel.
While we are dealing with this matter involving the widows in this particular tragedy there is something else I should like to bring to the attention of the committee, something which I think is a damnable insult to the widows of all sailors in Canada. It is something which should have been expunged from the statute books many years ago.
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)
I should like to quote from the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, chapter 178, section 41.
Where it is found by the board-
The board is the Merchant Seamen Compensation Board established under this act.
-that the widow to whom compensation has been awarded is a common prostitute or is openly living with any man in the relation of man and wife without being married to him, the compensation to such widow may be discontinued or suspended-
And so on. I Think it is most insulting that this should be found in the statute law of Canada because the implication is too clear to escape, namely, that all wives of sailors in this nation might become, as the act says, common prostitutes or might enter into a relationship with another man without being married to him.
That sort of archaic provision in our law should be removed. The Department of Veterans Affairs took steps in this direction some years ago not only to bring their law up

March 25, 1969
Supply-Transport
to date but also to recognize for the purpose of pensions the social fact in our society that men and women sometimes do live together without benefit of clergy. I say that all sailors' wives are placed in a position where a stigma is attached to them by this very section of the act. The widows of these unfortunate men who lost their lives because of the stinginess and lack of action on the part of the Canada Steamship Lines also are placed in the position of having this stigma attached to them. If we could repeal this provision now it would not be too soon.
So far as the amount of money accruing to the widows is concerned, $75 a month, it is insignificant compared with what is payable under the compensation laws that exist in my own province and other provinces.
I have expressed certain thoughts about the sinking of the ship itself. I should now like to refer to a few sections in Mr. Justice Gibson's report where he refers to the cause or causes of the capsizing and sinking and certain events leading up to it. With regard to the stability of the ship Mr. Justice Gibson says at page 6 of the report:
-it is probable that this vessel was properly loaded when it left Hamilton which is the last port at which cargo was taken aboard prior to its voyage to Montreal-except that too much weight was stowed in 'tween deck and on the spar deck with a minimum of ballast on board making the vessel tender and giving it a GM of 7 inches when it left Hamilton.
This is a technical reference to its degree of stability or instability. The reference to "tender" here is a common one when referring to a ship which is unstable or is on the verge of being topheavy and thus difficult to control. In subsequent parts of his report he deals more fully with this matter indicating that the ship listed to starboard and then to port and back again and this was corrected as a result of a considerable amount of effort in pumping water into the ballast tanks.
On page 8 of his report Mr. Justice Gibson has this to say with regard to the ballast. This is important and it is a contributing factor to the cause of the ship sinking. He speaks first about certain statistical information relating to the drums or tanks numerically and other matters. Then he says:
These facts are particularly significant as will appear later in this report because the action taken in respect to discharging some of this water ballast together with the opening of certain of the cargo doors in conjuncture was the cause of this casualty.

I should point out that the cargo doors to which he refers are 10 feet by 11 feet in diameter, that there are four of them on each side of the ship, that they are located in such a way as to be relatively close to the water line rather than on the top of the deck as is the case with ships that load and unload through cargo hatches, and that this was quite a contributing factor to this tragedy.
I want to point out now what occurred just prior to the ship capsizing and sinking. First, it pulled into the dock at Montreal in the early hours of the mornng around three o'clock. It takes about 20 minutes to tie up a ship of this kind. The crew is aroused from bed to come out on deck and assist in tieing up the ship, which they did. Canada Steamship Lines, by policy direction to its master, decided that they would use the seamen who had already been aroused to tie up the ship to open the cargo doors also, and they opened four on one side and two on the other. In this way Canada Steamship Lines got around having to pay extra for the opening of the doors.
Mr. Justice Gibson goes on to point out that it was this opening of the cargo doors which contributed to the sinking of the ship. I submit that Canada Steamship Lines was stingy in trying to save $12 which is what it would have cost to have left the cargo doors closed until such time as the load on the top deck had been taken off which affected the potential topheaviness. They should have left the doors closed at that time and waited until the longshore crew were there in the morning to open the doors after the load of steel on the top deck had been taken off. Twelve dollars equated with the lives of five Canadian sailors does not balance the scales so far as I am concerned.
One of the questions which the commission had posed to it related to the matter of the culpability which might be assessed to any person. Question No. 16 was:
Was the capsizing, fire and subsequent sinking of the Fort William caused or contributed to by the wrongful act or default of the owners, the master or any other person or persons?
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Mr. Justice Gibson's unequivocal answer was:
The owner for the reasons more specifically set out in the main body of the report.
He refers not to the master or any other person but to the owner, Canada Steamship Lines, which contributed to the capsizing, the
March 25, 1966

fire and the sinking of this ship by a wrongful act or default. There is no question in his mind at all about that aspect of it. Later he goes into this question further, as if there was any doubt about it, by referring to the opening of the cargo doors at the same time as the water was being pumped out of the ballast tanks in order to raise the ship in the water so the cargo doors and the top deck would be at the same level as the area of the dock for unloading purposes.
In regard to the pumping out of the ballast tanks in order that the ship would rise in the water Mr. Justice Gibson has something to say at page 21. Incidentally, in pumping out the water from the ballast tanks the ship not only rose but it became top heavy and consequently became unstable and tipped over. Mr. Justice Gibson says:
While the pumping abovementioned was taking place the cargo doors should have been left closed. It is of vital importance that the cargo doors be left closed and in the instant case even though the above suggested procedure of pumping tanks was not carried out, it is the opinion of R. P. Burnside, the expert called from the Department of Transport, that probably the vessel would not have capsized.
The assessors also advise and I accept their opinion that in the instant case also before any pumping was done and before the cargo doors were open the spar deck cargo should have been discharged first.
There is absolutely no question about that. He follows that up later by talking about the matter of pumping and the effect this had on the ship. On page 8 of the report he says:
As will appear later in this report it is what took place in connection with this pumping which created free surface water and caused this vessel to lose its equilibrium.
Let us consider what he means in terms of the construction of this ship. In the first place, it was built in a shipyard owned by Canada Steamship Lines, the same company which owned the vessel. It is interesting to note in this regard that the steamship line is going to be one of the greatest beneficiaries of the government's decision to reduce the vessel construction subsidy.
James Richardson and Sons refer to Canada Steamship Lines in dealing with this situation in a report in March, 1966, and state:
The government shipbuilding subsidy was reduced this January from 35 per cent to 25 per cent. Beginning January 1st, 1969, further reductions of 2 per cent will be made annually until the subsidy is reduced to 17 per cent. The cuts will place severe pressure on marginal yards and improve Canada Steamship Lines' competitive position.
Supply-Transport
Canada Steamship Lines owns the shipyard that built the Fort William.
It is considered normal and safe practice to have baffles placed in the ballast tanks in such a way that they are parallel to the keel of the ship. In other words, they run longitudinally so that when the water is in the process of being pumped out of the ship there will be an even distribution of weight contributing to the stability of the ship.
Mr. Justice Gibson says that as water is pumped out of the ballast tanks there is free surface water in the ballast tanks concentrated at one side of the bottom in the angle created by the keel and the hull of the ship. He says that this contributed to the list of the ship, be it on the port or starboard side. The free surface water would tend to move by the force of gravity to the side of the ship which was listing, thus contributing to its capsizing. So in effect the pumping out of these ballast tanks, because of faulty and unsafe construction of the ship, actually contributed to the ship capsizing by reason of the additional amount of weight on the listing side.
A very interesting part of this report deals with the loading of the ship. At page 10 and subsequent pages Mr. Justice Gibson points out that the master of the ship has no knowledge whatever of the loading of the ship, its cargo, the weight of the cargo or the manner in which the cargo is loaded. No officer is in a position to have sufficient knowledge about the cargo to assess the degree of stability or instability of the ship as a result of the loading of the cargo.
Mr. Justice Gibson refers to the loading and stowing of cargo and on page 10 he says:
The evidence clearly indicates that the shed for-men and the terminal superintendents at the various ports in the waters where this vessel traded loaded this vessel and all vessels of the owner. The vessel's officers in the practice of this trade carried on by the owner had practically nothing to say about the loading of cargo on this vessel. Clearly the vessel's officers did not know at any time prior to visiting any port the nature of the cargo to be loaded or its weight.
He expands on this point and states at page 11:
As a consequence, the seaworthiness of this vessel at any material time after loading was for all practical purposes assumed by the shore personnel.
As a result, the master or the first mate at any material time was left in almost difficult if not an impossible position in so far as being provided with adequate information to enable them or either of them to make any precise calculation of the stability of the vessel.

March 25. 1966
Supply-Transport
At page 12 in reference to written orders as to loading of the vessels he states:
There were no written standing orders regarding the loading of the vessel or the seaworthiness of the vessel after loading. The only written orders from the owners were concerning proper stowage of cargo to avoid claims for cargo damage from third parties.
There was no concern about the seaworthiness of the ship. There was no concern about the lives of the people who sailed her and no concern whatsoever about humanity. Apparently the only concern was in respect of dollars and cents. As the result of the exercise of that selfish attitude Canada Steamship Lines participated in the murder of five sailors on September 14, 1965.
I could go on and read other extracts from this report about loading and causes contributing to this accident, all of which would be expansions of those factors to which I have referred.
There is another matter regarding the manning of this ship to which I want to refer. Up until three years ago there was a certain minimum standard in regard to ship personnel. Three years ago Canada Steamship Lines decided that it had sufficient crews on its ships if they had one deck officer, which is all they had in this case, one wheelsman, which is all they had in this case, and one engineer, which is all they had in this case. They only had three officers, the deck officer, the wheelsmen and the engineer.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Let us see what happened after the ship had tied up. Orders were issued to start pumping out the ballast tanks in order that the ship would rise and be level with the area of the dock for purposes of unloading. Unloading was to start at seven o'clock that morning, some three hours later. The wheelsman, who I think had worked four days for that company, was on deck supervising the pumping of the ballast tanks. The engineer was down in the engineroom operating the pumps. There was a telephone at the control panel in the engineroom. There are sets of pumps in the engineroom for the ballast tanks, one set on the port side and one on the starboard side.
When the instructions were given to start pumping certain tanks, because the ship was so tender, in other words, so close to its equilibrium being upset because of the topheaviness of the cargo, the wheelsman on deck by telephone communication with the engineer-incidentally, the deck officer was

not paying any attention to what was going on; he was carrying out his duties and making up the manifest-said that the engineer could start pumping a certain tank. The engineer had to take that communication on the telephone, go down some steps in the engineroom and proceed to the particular area where the controls for the pumps were located.
As the engineer started to pump on one side the ship heeled over because as water was removed from the ballast tanks the ship rose in the water, lost its equilibrium and the topheaviness of the ship became more pronounced. The order was then issued by the wheelsman to stop pumping on that side and start pumping on the other side.
The engineer had to run up from one set of pumps, answer the telephone, go down to the other set of pumps and start them and carry on this process, all the while contributing to the death of five people because of the instructions and the stinginess of Canada Steamship Lines. I will not go into any more detail on this matter because I am sure it is easy for hon. members to see that with the deck officer busy with the manifest, one man up on deck watching the ship from side to side and one engineer in the engine room trying to operate the pumps, the ship being in a condition of tenderness which was known ever since the ship had left Hamilton, they could do nothing else but capsize the vessel if they persisted in carrying out the order to pump out those tanks, which they did. When the vessel listed over far enough on one side water entered the open cargo hatches and contributed further to the capsizing of the vessel. Canada Steamship Lines, guilty as they are, did not even have their wrists slapped because they were simply ordered to pay money.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
