Mr. Chairman, I am glad we have got the cargo loaded and unloaded on that particular ship. I have been waiting for two and a half hours to try to start building an airport. In previous speeches I have had the opportunity of delivering in this house I have outlined many of the problems that exist in the upper Ottawa valley in general and in Renfrew county in particular. I should like to say that I appreciate the sympathetic hearing I have received from the ministers concerned with these matters.
March 25, 1966

At Chalk River in Renfrew North we have the plant of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Because of the nature of this plant many scientists find it necessary on various occasions to travel to and from conferences at the plant. Personnel come to the plant from various universities not only in Canada but abroad. This necessitates a requirement for an improvement in transportation and particularly more rapid transportation. An airport is the transportation facility which I have in mind.
Twelve miles from the Atomic Energy plant at Chalk River there is the Petawawa military camp which is now the home base for the special mobile force. The existing facilities at Petawawa military base are being improved and repaired but there is a great possibility that more adequate air facilities will be needed for a camp such as is planned at Petawawa. In previous speeches I have also informed the house that we lack adequate transportation into and out of the area. This is a great hinderance to the business community.
With all these factors in mind, more adequate transportation for Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd., more adequate transportation for the military base at Camp Petawawa -both these enterprises are of great importance to our area-and the need for more rapid transportation for the business community, I should like to impress upon the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport, the Minister of National Defence and the Associate Minister of National Defence the importance of this facility and ask them to take into very serious consideration the establishment of perhaps a joint Department of Transport-Department of National Defence airport in the Pembroke-Petawawa-Deep River area.
At the present time there is a small airport in this area but its facilities are certainly not capable of handling traffic of the nature that I have been discussing. I do not know whether there have been precedents in the past whereby governments have entered into arrangements with private enterprise to develop air bases, but if this is the case there is certainly the potential in the area to warrant such a development. The management are more than willing to expand their facilities and co-operate in any way possible. If the Prime Minister and the ministers concerned would take this suggestion into consideration and at some future date put it into effect,
Supply-Transport
the people of Renfrew county would indeed be grateful.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, as a new member of the house I may take a minute of its time to deal with a matter of a different nature. I should like to address my remarks to every member in this chamber. As a new member I should like to compliment my colleagues upon the greatly improved attitude of mind that has existed here during the past week. It would be a wonderful situation if we could at all times sit in this house and make progress in matters that vitally affect our nation such as national unity, the future of the Canadian people and the dignity of this nation in the eyes of the world. These matters should be taken to heart by us at all times.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
As a young member of the house I should like to appeal to all my colleagues to face up to 1967 with a co-operative, humanitarian attitude, one that has only the best interests of our nation and the future of Canada and her people at heart. After our one hundredth birthday the people of Canada can then look back and say that while the twenty seventh parliament ran into some severe difficulties the members of that parliament had the ability to pick up the pieces and go on in a spirit of co-operation and national unity for the benefit of Canada as a whole and that they did indeed show the world that the Canadian people have initiative and drive and that we can live up to the humanitarian principles involved in the various religious faiths to which we belong.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that my colleagues were touched by the passionate appeal from the hon. member who just resumed his seat.
For my part, you may be assured of my co-operation if ever you should need it.
With regard to the estimates of the Department of Transport, I should like to make a few comments that could apply to all departments, all crown corporations and all public corporations.

For the last 15 years, Mr. Chairman, the municipal councils, Chambers of Commerce, both junior and senior, and the school boards of my home town and riding have been writing to the various federal departments to underline the fact that the name of my home city is Trois-Rivieres. This is true even in

Maich 25. 1966
Supply-Transport
spite of the English version because the city is incorporated under the name of Trois-Rivieres. A proper name is not translated and it is a grammatical error to translate a proper name. For instance, the name of our Speaker is Mr. Lamoureux but I would not speak of him in English as Mr. Lover. Mr. Batten is an English name but 1 would not call him Mr. Planchette if I were speaking French to him. We have a minister by the name of Mr. Winters but I would not call him Mr. Hiver if I were speaking to him in French. The name of my riding is Trois-Rivieres and I do not know how many hundred times we have to emphasize that fact.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Yes, sir.
I wonder why it is then that so many people from the province of Quebec insist on calling my fair city "Van-couvair"?

The hon. member should realize that this is perhaps because they are not used to the English pronunciation. When I speak English I call it Vancouver. I say "Paree" in French but I say "Paris" in English. If I want to speak to Mr. Lamontagne I do not call him Mr. Mountain in English, This is a mistake.
I know that many people from my riding have written to ministers about this name. I have several times communicated with the Minister of Transport about this mistake. I should like the ministers to give their departments instructions about the proper name.

May I rise on a question of privilege? My question of privilege relates to the hon. member for Renfrew North. I wanted to ask the hon. member not to leave his place because he made some comments at the opening of his speech with which I feel I must deal. I should like to have him present when I reply and I see he is about to leave. I would appreciate it if he remained.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. May I suggest that there is no question of privilege here? If the hon. member wishes to communicate with another hon. member he should do so by some other means rather than through the Chair.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to point out that the comment I have just made

was not inspired by narrow-mindedness. My hon. colleagues will realize that, even if our city is the second largest French speaking city in North America, its people took the trouble to learn English and to speak it well enough to communicate with our fellow-citizens in all the other provinces.
But the pride we show in wanting our city's name to be expressed in our mother tongue should not be held against us.
If I mention that while the estimates of the Department of Transport are being discussed, it is because I am afforded the opportunity. However, I should like to make the same comment with regard to all departments and I shall deem it my duty, in the next few days, to send a letter or memo to all ministers asking them to kindly give the required instructions so that the name of my home town and of my constituency are not to be changed at every opportunity.
You see it on trucks, in literature, in correspondence, and it does not please the people, even those who are English speaking.
Mr. Chairman, I listened a little earlier to the hon. member who was asking the Department of Transport to give him an airport in his region. I told him he could count on my co-operation, if it could be useful to him; it was promising him a lot. I just want to say that he is perfectly right. We are getting deeper and deeper into the century of aviation. I say that not only to support his request, because I know very well that it is important for the economy of the country, but also to point out that I have had previously the occasion to mention that we have a magnificent airport in Trois-Rivieres and that it would be important to extend the runway in the months to come, in view of Expo '67, as mentioned a little earlier by my hon. friend.
The airport in Trois-Rivieres will necessarily become an auxiliary airport for Montreal because the airports in Montreal will not be sufficient while Expo '67 is on.
We are about 80 miles from Montreal but there is no doubt that the big airliners coming from all over the world will be rerouted either to Trois-Rivieres or Sherbrooke.
The runway at our airport is 6,000 feet long. It is known that a length of 8,000 feet is required to accommodate some of those big airliners.
I would ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) for the second or third time to grant special attention to that request to
March 25, 1966

extend the runway in order to improve the situation in view of the needs for Expo '67.
I have something else to say but I will not be long. It is about the problem-and again I am bringing it up for the third time, I wrote and will write again about it until the problem is solved-which concerns my riding as well as the country's economy, since it is about our elevators and our grain which is shipped throughout the world, that grain which comes from the west and is shipped by railway. Operations have been going on at full capacity for several years. But over the last few months a misunderstanding has been dividing the administrators of the grain elevators and the municipality of Trois-Rivieres, concerning which the Minister of Transport has already intervened, since a delegation of the National Harbours Board came to our city to meet the municipal council and the parties concerned.
But things drag on. We have yet to find a solution. Not that I want to insinuate that the Department of Transport or the National Harbours Board are solely to blame. It is possible, though I do not wish to pass judgment, that the municipality did not act as diligently as it should have, but the fact remains that the problem with regard to the operations of our grain elevators is acute.
An important sector of our economy in greater Trois-Rivieres and the area, as well as an important part of the services which export western wheat through our area, are being jeopardized by this imbroglio.
I should like to insist again with the minister that he use all his influence with a view to expediting, if at all possible, the solution to the problems of grain elevators at Trois-Rivieres.
Another point, Mr. Chairman, and I shall resume my seat. I apologize for insisting, but we, newcomers, are precisely taking advantage of the fact that our audience is enthusiastic in the house to express our complaints.
We already had the opportunity to refer to an appointment made by the National Harbours Board. The manager of national harbours was appointed and, at the time, I maintained the appointment smacked of patronage or protection if you prefer. I am of those who believe appointments should be made according to certain standards.
For instance, I feel that within the public service qualifications and seniority should be taken into account. But if they are not, Mr. Chairman, if there is to be patronage in my
Supply-Transport
riding, then, I want to be the one to dispense favours, and I do not want to leave it to public servants; my stand is as simple and clear as that.
But still I advocate the observance of some standards which, for instance, are accepted in the civil service, that is that account be taken of the experience, education and number of years of service of the candidate. With this, I agree.
Now, I say that, until otherwise proven, this is not what was done in the appointment of a national harbours board manager at Trois-Rivieres.
There are, at the national harbours board, several employees with 10, 15 and 20 years of service, while the appointee had only five.
I was told, on one occasion, that he was an engineer and that, because of developments in the port of Trois-Rivieres, it was imperative that he should be an engineer.
I know engineers with 10, 12 or 15 years experience at the national harbours board who would have filled that position more ably.
There is something I do not understand about this appointment, and I intend to talk about it, not because I have something against the present incumbent-I realize he must make a living like everybody else-but because I know that there is involved, Mr. Chairman, a matter of principle that has always been recognized in this house, that is promotions and appointments must be on the basis of qualifications, experience and seniority. And I would like the same process to apply in this case as in all other cases. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make one comment on the remarks made by the hon. member for Renfrew North and ask, him to reflect, if he would, on what he said at the beginning of his remarks. I say this for fear of his own safety. I have been dealing with the matter of safety on ships but if his comments remain on Hansard in the way he said them I think they could leave him open to a great deal of criticism. I am sure he did not meant to impart what I took from his remarks.
I think I have almost his exact words. He said he was glad that the ship to which I had been making reference had had its cargo loaded and unloaded because he had been waiting for some two and a half hours to

March 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
make a comment about an airport, I would simply point out to the hon. member that I would not want the impression to get abroad that he was disdainful of or disinterested in this ship and what took place with regard to it. I point out to him that the cargo of that ship was unloaded but in a most tragic fashion.
The ship listed to one side, dumping some of the cargo into the water and the rest of it between decks to one side of the ship thus bringing about sparks, an explosion, the death of five people and the sinking of the ship. That is the manner in which the cargo was unloaded and I merely mention it in the hope that the hon. member will, if he so desires, reflect on what he said and at some subsequent time clear up what may be a very bad interpretation placed on his remarks. I would not want people to think unkindly of him as a result of those remarks having appeared on Hansard.
Before my time expired earlier I had got to the stage of the imposition of penalties by the court of investigation into the sinking of the Fort William. A penalty was imposed on Canada Steamship Lines which was found to be negligent in its operation of the ship. As a penalty the court ordered the owner to pay part of the costs of investigation up to $10,000.
I submit that that is not even a slap on the wrist to a company like the Canada Steamship Lines with profits ranging into millions of dollars. That sort of penalty for its actions is really nothing more than a licence fee for that company to carry on in the same fashion of having its ships loaded at ports without the master or the mates of the ships having any knowledge of the distribution of the weight load. It is a licence fee for that company to continue to cut back on the manning of its ships and the watches on those ships to the point where they are manned by skeleton crews. It is a licence fee for that company to continue to build ships which are unsafe and in some conditions unmanageable. It is a licence fee for that company to continue to exploit its sailors all for the almighty buck. It is a licence fee for that company to continue its composite practices to the end that we may have another tragedy such as that which struck the Fort William and the people who worked upon her.
Perhaps no retroactive action can be taken but something can be done for the future. I said earlier that there was guilt on the part of the company. The court of investigation

under Mr. Justice Gibson proved that conclusively, and their guilt was set out throughout his report. I also think there is guilt on the part of the Minister of Transport and the government.
I notice that the hon. gentleman who in Hansard is referred to as Member of the Administration but who in common parlance is referred to as Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, is in the house. I understand that somehow he is an adjunct to the Minister or to the Department of Transport, so I hope that some time during the consideration of these estimates he will make some declaration of policy and interest on behalf of the government with respect to this matter.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I think that the government and the Minister of Transport are at least guilty of disinterest in having refused so far to promulgate regulations under section 410, if my memory serves me correctly, of the Canada Shipping Act in connection with manning requirements on ships. I think that the tragedy to which I have referred today shows conclusively that if there had been a sufficient minimum watch requirement on ships and one further unlicensed member of the crew had been on watch at four o'clock on the morning of September 14, perhaps this tragedy would not have occurred. Perhaps the lives of the five sailors would have been saved.
The statement of the wheelsman who was on watch was to the effect that if there had been one other person on watch with him he would have sent that other person to awaken the crew and prepare them to abandon ship because he sensed very clearly the tragedy which was about to happen. In his statement he indicated, as others had, that he was very scared. Some members of the crew were not even desirous of going to bed that night because of the situation which had prevailed on the ship ever since it left Hamilton. The situation was such that when they pulled up at the dock at Iroquois locks they were ordered by one of the officers controlling the locks to pull alongside and stabilize the ship or they would have to weigh anchor. He would not let the ship go through the locks. The crew had to pump all the ballast tanks full in order to put the ship low enough in the water for it to be stable.
The wheelsman and other crew members knew of the instability of the ship. They
March 25, 1966

knew of the potential danger and expressed concern when the order was given to pump out the ballast tanks with the cargo doors open. They knew what might result. If there had been one other person on the ship, if minimum manning requirements on a minimum basis had been established by the minister and the government under section 4(10) of the Canada Shipping Act, which specifically gives the government the right to make such regulations, perhaps the lives of five people would have been saved.
I say that the government is guilty of disinterest, if not of outright negligence, in procrastinating on the question of manning requirements under the Canada Shipping Act.
I say that the government is guilty of disinterest in allowing an almost archaic Canada Shipping Act to remain on the statute books. The Canada Shipping Act provisions are responsible partly for the type of court of investigation. The act is responsible for the fact that certain unlicensed personnel on that ship were not permitted to appear before that court as parties and accordingly were not permitted to have counsel represent them. This is partly the result of having a Canada Shipping Act which is long overdue for overhaul.
To give an example of what I mean, I was reading a section of the act in which there is reference to certain types of screwdriven and other steamships which, on August 26, 1889, had certain factors attributable to them and the section specifies that they shall be dealt with in a certain way. Mr. Chairman, 1889, is a long time ago. I doubt that any ships that were plying the lakes in 1889 are currently plying the St. Lawrence or any of the waters of Canada or any other trade routes. Provisions of this sort are found in the Canada Shipping Act. The one to which I have referred is indicative of sections throughout the act which are absolutely archaic and which relate to the time of Admiral Nelson of the British navy.
The act is completely out of date. It does not take cognizance of current day shipping factors and it should be overhauled. The act should be cleaned out from stem to stern and brought up to date.
I say that there is a clear and unequivocal responsibility upon the shoulders of the government to do this. The Minister without Portfolio is here and, to use his own words, he was seconded by minister or by the department. I do not know which statement
Supply-Transport
would be more applicable. I think there is a responsibility upon the hon. gentleman to give some indication to the committee what the government's or his own intentions are with respect to studying and modernizing the Canada Shipping Act.
I think there is also a responsibility devolving perhaps not on him but on the government with respect to the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act which in a denigrating way refers to the widows of sailors and classifies them as potentially common tarts. This is the sort of inheritance in our law that should be removed so that we can have an up to date Canada Shipping Act which takes cognizance of the matters I have mentioned with which we are concerned. In particular and overriding all else, there must be established some sort of accident prevention rules or safety precaution methods. The lives of Canadians are involved in the Canada Shipping Act. Five lives were lost on September 14, 1965, because of arrogant stinginess and negligence on the part of Canada Steamship Lines and because of disinterest on the part of this and other governments.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words to endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Skeena and also to indicate that members of the house are going to have to give consideration to safety on the Great Lakes. The Minister without Portfolio has spoken to the house about the problem of safety and that, of course, is probably where I came in.
I attended a meeting not long ago that the minster arranged. It was of a fairly technical nature and the discussion concerned safety on the Great Lakes. I was surprised to find that the shipping companies, the pilots, the representatives of the S.I.U., the tug boat companies, the representative of the people concerned with shipping on both the Great Lakes and the seaway, were pretty well in agreement as to what should be done. They said what ought to be done was going to cost the government some money. They were talking of providing v.h.f. radio equipment immediately for the beginning of the season.
What really surprised and shocked me was that the Department of Transport said, "No, no, no" or "but, but, but". Everybody else agreed that certain things should be done in this way or that way. However, immediately that was said the deputy minister jumped up and said: But we cannot do it for this reason or for that reason. Finally he made the idiotic

March 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
statement that we did not own the waterway, that everything below Montreal is in international waters and the government of Canada can do nothing about it.
If this is true, I think the hon. member who spoke-I believe he is from Three Rivers-will find himself in one of the areas far beyond-
May I ask a question?

Wait till I finish-he will find himself in the position of being on the international waterway and not on what we consider to be the St. Lawrence Seaway. If we cannot call it the seaway we can call it the St. Lawrence riverway, which we believe falls within the jurisdiction of the government of Canada.
Would you please allow a question? When the hon. member referred to Three Rivers did he mean my constituency? As I said when I spoke, it is Trois-Rivieres.

I stand corrected. It is Trois-Rivieres. If what the deputy minister said was true I presume that the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, being in an area below Montreal, would obviously be outside the federal jurisdiction. This might not matter to many members of parliament because most of them do not represent maritime areas. However, I was shocked to find representatives of the S.I.U. saying something which nobody has corrected if it is wrong. They said that over 10 per cent of S.I.U. members working on the Great Lakes last year were casualties. In other words, there were accidents to more than 10 per cent of all the people that the S.I.U. represented.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
Can you think of any other group of workers in any other field of endeavour who would accept one out of every ten employees in that industry being injured?
I think this is a record of which we certainly cannot be proud. The first thing is to convince the Department of Transport of the need to do something about it. I have listened to the technical arguments. I am no expert but I do know what was said was really an excuse for inaction. We were talking about something which would cost, at the extreme, not more than $50,000. I do not know how much the Minister of Transport considers the life of one seaman to be worth, but on this one ship which my hon. friend from Skeena was talking about, five lives 
were lost and I do not think anyone here would wish to put a price on those lives. I am not saying, of course, that expenditures in the interest of safety could have prevented this particular tragedy. Nevertheless I have read reports which strongly suggest that safer conditions generally would be brought about if there were a more positive program on the part of the department.
It surprised me to learn there are no logs kept on ships engaged in Great Lakes traffic. If I were, say, an able seaman on a ship sailing outside the Great Lakes I would be in a position to make a complaint about the condition of any part of the ship which fell within my own responsibility. I could have an entry made in the ship's log accordingly and my own responsibility would be removed or diminished. The subject of the complaint would then become a matter for investigation and action by a higher authority. But the Department of Transport does not license ships on the Great Lakes. Mr. Chairman, your wife could go down and become a helmsman on the Great Lakes as long as somebody would hire her. And if the price was right, they probably would.
If I had sailed for 20 years on the lakes and it appeared to me that a certain ship was unsafe, do hon. members know what I would have to do? I would have to go to a customs officer, ask for an inspection and deposit total demurrage in respect of the time the ship was laid up awaiting and undergoing inspection. I would have to put up $20,000 in cash before I could ask for an inspection, no matter what my qualifications might be.
My hon. friend from Skeena has pointed out what happens when an inquiry is held. The seamen have no right to counsel; they have no right to cross-examine. This has been the case for years under the mining act in Ontario which has long been considered to be an archaic piece of legislation designed to protect the companies rather than the workers. Under that legislation, too, the miners were never asked the questions necessary to elicit answers upon which a reasonable conclusion could be based. They were asked questions by the inspectors, who were always considered to be acting in the interest of the mining companies rather than of the miners. They only asked questions which were likely to produce the answers they wanted to hear. In the case which was brought to our attention by my hon. friend, the employees are similarly not given any right to cross-examine and the information they are able to give
March 25, 1966

is seldom presented, unless by accident when an inquiry officer makes a mistake.
This is an important topic. Canada is becoming more and more dependant each year on trade through the Great Lakes. This trade is increasing rapidly, yet we are unwilling to face the fact that the Canada Shipping Act belongs to the old sailing days rather than to the modern diesel age or even to the age of steam. Everything but cutlasses is discussed in this legislation. It should be amended, and amended immediately. I am sure that after listening to this debate the minister will tell us that though he is in favour of doing something we should first consider the matter for a very long time. But if the unions are not to be forced into taking drastic action by supporting a walkout every time they consider conditions to be unsafe, we ourselves must introduce the changes in the shipping act which will enable the Department of Transport to do the policing which it is now charged with doing, but which it is incapable of doing. There are only 11 inspectors, I am told, to deal with all the shipping on the Great Lakes. Thus, if an inspection is called for it may be several days before an inspector can get to the port, and the demurrage charge makes the whole procedure impractical.
I was interested to hear that officials of the department are interested in this v.h.f. equipment which they feel constitutes a useful safety measure. It was pointed out that this year an international safety agreement has been negotiated to which Canada is a signatory. We were told a meeting will take place in the near future at which Canada will be represented by the deputy minister of transport. I believe that, whoever represents Canada, this meeting should urge that a change be made as soon as possible to allow Canada to have some control over the type of equipment being used on the St. Lawrence River, particularly in those areas not now served by v.h.f.-the area below the port of Montreal. Unless we are able to put before that meeting specific information as to what changes are considered desirable so that shipping from all parts of the world may be able to equip themselves with the necessary permanent radio installations, there cannot be much hope of early success and Canada will be bound to find some loophole, some means of bringing about this result by subterfuge. And I do not think this is the way in which this objective should be reached.
Supply-Transport
I hope the minister, when he replies, will tell us that the wishes at the safety meeting which I had the opportunity of attending will be communicated to this forthcoming conference by Canada's representative. I hope the views expressed at that meeting will be put forward in the strongest terms in order that some consideration may be given to the installation this year of permanent v.h.f. radio equipment on shipping not only in the lower St. Lawrence but throughout the Great Lakes, as is now required after joint negotiation between Canada and the United States.
I hope also that the minister is in a position to say that there will be amendments to the Canada Shipping Act-that the entire act will be revised and brought up to date, taking into consideration the many changes that have taken place and the obvious agreement which existed between the shipping companies and all parties interested in safety on the lakes, and in developing a much safer waterway this summer.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, at this time it to say that there will be amendments to the hon. member for Skeena. I wish to assure him that I am sufficiently humanitarian and pride myself on having enough of a conscience that I never would make the interpretation or deliver the insinuation he suggested I may have meant. Sitting over here I was under the impression, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Skeena ended up his speech talking about ships and conditions in general. I hope I am right in that. Hence, since my speech was dealing with airports I used this merely as an introduction to move from ships to planes. I can assure the hon. member and the committee that I had no intention whatsoever of giving the impression about which he commented after my address.

Mr. Chairman, in response to this, may I say that in no way did I wish to cast reflection upon the hon. gentleman, or make as he said any insinuation. I merely pointed out what others may take as an interpretation of what he said, and I did not want that interpretation to go abroad.

Mr. Chairman, just to clarify this whole matter, I should say that I appreciate the comment by the hon. member for Skeena, and certainly must say in closing that I appreciate the fact that he brought this to my attention, because I certainly would not want that thought to remain on Hansard. I thank him very sincerely.

March 25, 1966
Supply-Transport

Mr. Chairman, I also wish to deal with the matter of safety, and deal with a situation which may cause tragedies even more disastrous than the ones to which my colleague for Skeena referred earlier this afternoon.
On March 4 I first raised this matter in the House of Commons in the form of a question to the Minister of Transport. I raised the matter as a result of numerous telephone conversations and correspondence from air line pilots of my acquaintance, and later from official correspondence from the Canadian Airline Pilots Association, protesting against the decision of the International Civil Aviation Organization of last January to narrow the air lanes across the North Atlantic from 120 miles to 90 miles.
At that time the minister told me he would look into the matter and answer my question later. Ten days later, on March 14, he very kindly sent me a memorandum from the department in explanation of the position of the Canadian government in this dispute between the International Civil Aviation Organization and the Canadian Airline Pilots Association and the International Federation of Airline Pilots Associations.
In this memorandum, Mr. Chairman, there is this, which I find rather difficult to understand:
At the present time those pilots of international flights operating across the North Atlantic who accepted the new international standard of 90 miles, and I can assure you that they constitute a significant majority-
The reason I later attempted to ask the minister again another question in this regard is that the next day, on March 15, I found a report in the Globe and Mail of the meeting of the International Federation of Airline Pilots Associations in Auckland, New Zealand, at which they unanimously rejected this regulation as unsafe and decided to tell the 27,000 members of the various international airline pilots associations to refuse to comply with the new measures.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it would appear to me that the Minister of Transport has been receiving some rather faulty information. I would like to know who in the Department of Transport told the Minister of Transport that a significant majority of the air line pilots were prepared to accept the 90 mile air lane in the North Atlantic, because in the correspondence I have from the Canadian Airline Pilots Association, which substantiates the

news report, it becomes perfectly plain that unanimously this has been rejected.
I think this poses a very serious problem for this parliament. In this memorandum it says that at the meeting of the international aviation organizations-
-the meeting concluded that reduction of the standard to 90 miles could be accomplished with safety and incorporated in the report of the meeting and appropriate recommendation. This recommendation, supported by Canada, was subsequently endorsed by the ICAO Air Navigation Commission and finally approved by the council of ICAO. The new standard became effective on January 13, 1966.
So, we have here the evidence that our government has agreed to this narrowing of the air lanes across the North Atlantic from 120 miles to 90 miles in complete defiance of the decision of the only people whose opinions are worth a damn, and these are the jet pilots who fly these lanes; these are the men on whom the safety of the air line passengers depends.
I can only conclude, Mr. Chairman, that the government of Canada once again is following its usual policy of pusillanimous subservience to the wishes of an important major power which lies alongside of us, and its commercial representatives, and is callously indifferent to the opinions of the men who have to carry out this injunction or lose their jobs, and risk not only the lives of their passengers but also their own lives.
I suggest it is time this government learned to have a little courage and intelligence. The Airline Pilots Association agreed that the lanes could be narrowed to a very limited extent; they agreed it might be possible to narrow them by six nautical miles. The commercial interests are determined to narrow them by 30 miles, when there is ample evidence that in the best of conditions a jet plane flying at the immensely high rates of speeds at which they fly today can, say in the course of a split second, easily move up to 30 miles off course because of temporary failure of instruments. Yet our government by its own confession is prepared to fly in the face of this recommendation, the recommendation of the only people whose opinion is worth listening to, and the only people to whom we should listen.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I would implore the Minister without Portfolio to convey to the Minister of Transport the necessity of examining this matter very much more closely than he appears to
March 25. 1966

have done to date, and to listen very carefully not only to our own Canadian Airline Pilots Association but also to the international body, although I would like to note that our air line pilots have a reputation unsurpassed in the world for safety. It may well be that the government of Canada would be well advised to listen to these men rather than to commercial interests who want to increase the possibilities of making profits on North Atlantic flights.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay the business of the house, but I feel duty bound to take part in the discussion, since I have been asked to make representations in favour of Montreal harbour.
There now exists a situation which is detrimental to Montreal harbour and should be corrected, it seems to me, as soon as possible.
Arbitrary restrictions now being imposed by the Winnipeg Grain Exchange affect very unfavourably Montreal harbour's economy and thus, that of Montreal generally.
As a result of the restrictions laid down by the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, some grain elevators in Montreal remain empty for a long period at the beginning of the shipping season.
For instance, last year, because of those restrictions, elevator No. 1 was not in use for nine days, while elevator No. 3 was empty for eight days. Elevator No. 5 did not operate for nine days and elevator No. 4 for eight days.
The restrictions imposed by the Winnipeg Grain Exchange could have been explained by the situation which prevailed in past years, but since 1963, the building of an additional elevator in Montreal allows grain from foreign countries to be handled in the harbour.
I simply wish to ask briefly the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Turner), who is surely aware of the situation, to make the necessary representations in order to avoid any further inconvenience to Montreal harbour.
This discrimination against Montreal harbour has been going on too long to be tolerated any longer. Last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) I believe, had given the undertaking that negotiations would be continued to correct this situation but it seems that the staff of the Montreal Harbour board has not obtained satisfaction since their grievances are being made public.
Supply-Transport
I read in the Montreal Gazette lor March 23, the following heading:
Unfair to Montreal harbour.
And the article relates the discrimination which is going on through a body completely foreign to the economic life of Montreal harbour.
With my last words I would ask the Minister without Portfolio to do everything in his power to have this situation remedied.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few brief words about the supplementary estimates for the Department of Transport. I want to make it quite clear that I am speaking in my capacity as a private member, as a member who represents a coastal constituency with a number of shipyards and as a member from a part of Canada which pays a considerable volume of tax into the federal treasury.
We on the west coast are proud of many things, one of which is the new ferry system which the provincial government has built and has been operating since 1960 between the mainland and Vancouver Island. Many members on both sides of the house were concerned earlier this year when the announcement on shipbuilding subsidies was made. There was reference to a 25 per cent subsidy which would apply in respect of categories of ships operated by private enterprise, but government ships were specifically excluded. This change not only excluded vessels built on the federal government's account, but vessels built by provincial governments as well. Since the province of British Columbia is the only province which enters substantially into the construction and operation of ferries, this change appeared to many people to be a measure aimed specifically at British Columbia.
Let me point out another aspect of this problem. If the ferry system in the province of British Columbia was still operated by private enterprise that system would now be receiving the 25 per cent subsidy. In other words, as a result of this exclusion and because the provincial government moved into this area of activity, the people of British Columbia, who use this ferry service extensively, are being denied federal government tax support in respect of the construction of these ferries.
Over the past six years the federal government has committed more than $15 million of federal tax money to the construction of

March 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
these ferries in British Columbia. Approximately one third of their total cost has been met by the federal taxpayers. This program is nearing an end. Only one or two more ferries remain to be built and it seems to me to be a shame that the federal government has seen fit to cut off the subsidy when, for a modest additional amount of money, it could complete that program and take full credit for very substantial assistance in the creation of an important and very effective ferry system.
The number of dollars involved is large in the eyes of private individuals, but small relative to the total number of dollars being spent by the federal government in respect of similar services both within certain eastern provinces and as between various provinces on the Atlantic coast.
In this regard I need only refer to the recent report of the Auditor General in respect of intraprovincial ferry systems. At page 78 of the Auditor General's report he refers to terminal facilities which the federal government paid for at Matane and Godbout in Quebec. He states:
This acquisition has now brought to six the number of locations where the federal government has provided terminals at both ends of cross-river ferry services in the lower St. Lawrence river. The total expenditure over the years for these terminals, which in some cases form part of shipping wharves, had exceeded $7 million at March 31, 1965.
The federal government has also been providing substantial ferry services between the provinces in eastern Canada. This is a constitutional responsibility of the federal government and I certainly am not critical in that regard. Indeed I believe the federal government should assume responsibility in this regard and carry it out in an energetic way.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
But the order of magnitude of these amounts spent for ferry services is interesting. The Newfoundland ferry terminals deficit, for 1966-67 is shown in our estimates as $11.9 million as opposed to the sort of subsidy which would be required in British Columbia of the order of $2 million a year for ship construction. The Prince Edward Island car ferry and terminals deficit was $4.4 million. The cost of a ferry vessel for service between North Sydney and Argentia, Newfoundland, was $2.5 million. The cost of the ferry vessel for freight service between North Sydney, Nova Scotia, and Port aux Basques was $7.9 million. I could refer to numerous other

items, and still not include the more than $10 million for construction of dock and terminal facilities at places like Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, and North Sydney, Nova Scotia. These are very large amounts of money that run into tens of millions of dollars, and we are only asking for one or two million dollars a year for a couple of years in order to round out the federal subventions for transportation on the west coast.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to indicate the nature and scale of steamship subventions paid by the federal government for eastern local services. For 1966-67 they are estimated to be $8.7 million. For local services on the west coast of Canada the amount is $412,000; in other words, less than half a million dollars.
We in British Columbia pay taxes. Our costs and wages, generally speaking, are higher. We pay more taxes per capita. Most British Columbians feel they should get a fair shake in respect of the variety of services supplied by the federal government. Ferries perform a service in which we have considerable interest-an interest akin to that of people who live on our east coast. As both taxpayer and, in this instance, a member of parliament from the west coast I feel strongly that we should be treated on the same basis as those on the east coast.
I noticed with considerable interest that the Minister of Transport, when his main estimates were before this committee a few weeks ago, stated that it would not break his heart if he had to alter the regulations in so far as they apply to federal government assistance for provincially owned and constructed ferry systems. I am quite sure that if he would relent and modify these regulations he would gladden the hearts of a great many people in British Columbia. He would give the impression in British Columbia-and this feeling is quite widespread in certain circles-that British Columbia is not being discriminated against in this way.
I know that such modification of the regulations would also gladden the hearts of members on all sides of this house, regardless of party. Therefore I plead with the Minister of Transport and the Minister without Portfolio to take another hard look at the ship subventions, or ship subsidies, and permit the payment of these subsidies in respect of ferry vessels built on provincial government account.
March 25, 1966

Mr. Chairman, I rise briefly to support the remarks made by the hon. member tor Coast-Capilano. This is an indication of our changing society. Here is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister of Canada-
Not now.

-openly and willingly advocating the subsidization of publicly owned transportation. I think we can safely say that this means the Liberal party is now 50 per cent socialist, and I congratulate them on that account. I think the hon. member's argument was sound. It is not a question of the amount of money; I think it is the principle behind it. There is a feeling in British Columbia, regardless of party affiliation, that the provincial government should receive the same treatment as private companies building ships in this country.
I mention this, Mr. Chairman, because the government of British Columbia also builds ferries which operate in the Kootenays on the Arrow and Kootenay Lakes, and these ships would also come under subsidy if they were built in B.C. shipyards. With those few remarks I resume my seat, but I could not help congratulating the parliamentary secretary in view of the high position he holds in this land.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment briefly on some of the excellent contributions made during the discussion of these supplementary estimates, as they apply to the Department of Transport. I listened of course with great interest, as I always do, to the hon. member for Skeena. I am not going to comment on the report of the judicial inquiry into the tragedy of the Fort William except to deal with one particular aspect that was not really sub judice, but was a comment by the hon. member to the effect that the seamen involved were not allowed counsel at the inquiry.
I want to make it clear to the committee that it has been the practice at these inquiries to allow only those parties to appear who may be subject to sanctions or criticism, and since the seamen involved, and certainly their families, were in no way responsible for the tragedy that occurred, they were not intimately involved as parties to the inquiry. The owners and the officers whose certificates were subject to cancellation were involved as direct parties to the inquiry. There was no restriction, nor is there ever a restriction, on
Supp ly-Transport
seamen being represented by counsel with a watching brief. If at any time in the course of any inquiry it should appear that such seamen are likely to become blameworthy or in any way involved in a liability arising under such inquiry, then of course such counsel could at that time apply to the commissioner or the judge to have the seamen named as parties to the inquiry. Thereupon counsel have the right to participate in all the examination and cross-examination of the witnesses who appear before the inquiry.
I now leave that matter and come to the general subject of the Canada Shipping Act. I shall not go into detail in regard to that rather voluminous statute and deal with it section by section, except to say that it is under active review by the department. As far as my personal interest is concerned, having had on many, many occasions to try and interpret that statute in private practice, I could not agree more with the hon. member when he said that in several of its parts and sections it is entirely outmoded and ought to be revised. I was shocked to listen to the text of section 41 of the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act, which I agree is in terms highly insulting to seamen and their families. I must confess this was the first time that section had ever been recited to me.
On the general question of marine safety on the lakes, the St. Lawrence river and the channel out to the ocean, I would say in answer to the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Timiskaming that we have now reached a stage where it is no longer a question of policy but rather one of technicality and technique in working out the best means, in co-operation with industry and the unions, to achieve by way of a reasonable set of priorities as quickly as we can a safer sea lane and river lane into the heart of this continent.
I want to say that progress cannot be made, as I am sure hon. members will realize, in all directions at once. We have therefore laid out what we think is a reasonable set of priorities, hoping to achieve as soon as we can those systems of traffic information and traffic control which we believe have the earliest chance of success. It is because we now feel that in the realm of communications and traffic information we are in the position to instal a permanent system of v.h.f. radio on the river from Les Escoumains right up to Montreal that we intend to instal such a system.

March 25. 1966
Supply-Transport
* (3:40 p.ra.)
Some members may know that on an experimental and temporary basis over the past months there has been a mobile radio communications network on the river. It has proved to be successful and we are now in the position to instal it on a permanent basis. This means that there will be available a series of concurrent, very high frequency radio communications systems up and down the river which will be available to all ships going up and down the channel. That is merely a first stage. It allows every ship to pinpoint its position as it goes up or down the channel. It enables the Department of Transport to advise every ship as to the positions of other ships either below or up river. In that sense, traffic information will be the first step toward achieving, I hope, a better safety record on the St. Lawrence river.
Now, of course, the obvious question that members of the committee would ask me, Mr. Chairman, is: If there is going to be v.h.f. radio on the shore, how will the department be able to communicate with those oceangoing vessels which are not equipped with such an installation? As mentioned by the hon. member for Timiskaming, it is compulsory for ships plying the Great Lakes and the seaway to use v.h.f. radio. This is the result of a treaty between the United States and Canada which was excepted from the provisions of the IMCO treaty already mentioned. However, the compulsory features of this agreement excepted under the United Nations agency are not applicable below Montreal, so the compulsory features with regard to v.h.f. radio stop at the seaway and at the Great Lakes.
The difficulty Canada faces is that, being a party to the IMCO agreement, we have to persuade the other maritime nations of the world to adopt the use, on a compulsory basis, of v.h.f. radio on their vessels so that we can communicate bridge to bridge and shore to ship, thus rendering effective all the precautions we are taking on the river. The suggestion the hon. member made that at the next meeting of IMCO Canada take a very strong position in this respect is, of course, already part of our own thinking. I can assure the house that the assistant deputy minister of transport, marine, will take with him to that meeting the instructions of the Canadian government to achieve if he can the

consent of the international body to the installation on a compulsory basis of v.h.f. radio on the bridges of all ships. However, this provision needs the ratification of over two thirds of the signatory nations to the treaty. I cannot, at the moment, forecast how quickly we will be able to achieve that majority.
In the meantime, the department has been experimenting with portable v.h.f. radios which can be brought on the vessels by the pilots as they enter the river. The fee for the use of the radio would, of course, be added to the pilotage fee which the owners or charterers of the vessels would have to pay. The difficulty at the moment is that the range of these portable radios is still very limited, not more than five miles, although we are hoping that a new type of instrument has been developed which will give us more range. I hope that we can foresee the day when either we will have this type of portable equipment which we can make compulsory by way of pilots taking it on board vessels, or that we can achieve the co-operation of owners of vessels that ply the St. Lawrence river into Montreal, or that eventually we can persuade the other maritime nations of the world to accept this kind of equipment on a compulsory basis.
Once we have compulsory high frequency radio installed, then not only will we have a means of ship-to-ship and ship-to-shore communication all the way up and down the river, but we will have an information centre operating on the river advising the position of every vessel thereon. We will be able to achieve then what I think is absolutely necessary in view of the tremendous increase in traffic, namely a traffic control system whereby we will be able to say to the various vessels either "Hold your position until the channel clears," or "You may now proceed". In other words, we will have a series of red and green lights by way of high frequency radio up and down the channel.
There were many representatives of maritime interests at the meeting with their own particular briefs. The two-channel concept was stressed very strongly. The Dominion Marine Association and the Seafarers International Union pressed this point. As a result of the meeting which we had in Montreal, I think all parties agree now that it would be better to widen the channel from ]VIontreal to Quebec rather than to put in a two channel system. This is true not only from a safety but from a hydraulic point of
Match 25, 196G

view. We are deeply concerned that if we double the channel in the river between Montreal and Quebec we will accelerate the flow to such an extent that the water level at the port of Montreal could not be maintained. We are looking into these factors by means of our new hydraulic model at La Salle which we hope to open next month. We will continue our studies of the water level' and the double channel problem.
Below Quebec and tie d'Orleans, there is a problem in using the south channel. We are using our engineering data now, but as soon as the ice clears up we intend to carry out a survey of current and tide and the texture of the soil to see if this idea can be implemented from an engineering point of view. I just want to say here that I take a most serious view of the situation on the St. Lawrence river. The Minister of Transport and I intend to continue our series of meetings with interested parties in the maritime business. We intend to hold another meeting at the end of April to discuss possible channel problems and we hope that by implementing these ideas, in co-operation with the industry, with the underwriters, unions and other parties involved, we will be able to improve the record of safety on the St. Lawrence.
I wanted to deal briefly with a comment made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands about the narrowing of the air lanes over the North Atlantic from 120 to 90 miles. This provision of course was implemented by the International Civil Aviation Organization with the consent, as I understand it, of all the major air nations of the world. I am advised that the reason behind the move is the tremendous increase in the volume of traffic crossing the Atlantic and the limited space available. Some changes had to be made if traffic were to continue to move. I am advised that all the evidence points this amendment as safe.
In any event, I am personally going to look into the brief of the pilots association which was referred to by the hon. member, to see what merit there is in it. I am advised that the majority of international pilots have not objected to this particular measure.
In answer to the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-

I may say that on April 4, a delegation from Montreal will come here to the capital city to meet with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Supply-Transport
Pickersgill), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) and myself to discuss, before the official opening of navigation, the system of priorities used at present for Canadian grain.
[English1
I want to say that I have spent a good deal of my time in the last few weeks looking into this problem of the relative priorities of export grain from the port of Montreal. At the moment, absolute priority is given by regulation of the Board of Grain Commissioners for the export of Canadian grain prior to the opening of the season at the Lakehead. There is a strong argument to be made, and it has been made on behalf of the port of Montreal, that with the capacity of the elevators there and the fact that private elevators at other ports along the river now are not subject to the same absolute prohibition but are allowed to take in grain on a 60-40 ratio, Canadian-United States, this regulation should be annulled. However, I am not in a position to say more.
[DOT] (3:50 p.ra.)

Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the comments of the Minister of Transport.
Oh, I am sorry; I listened with such interest that I assumed that he was the Minister of Transport, so I will not apologize for my incorrect description of the Minister without Portfolio.
However, I would ask him to consider one further matter with regard to any formal investigations conducted under the Canada Shipping Act, with specific reference to the Fort William to which he has just referred. I am talking about something more than inquiries; I am talking about formal investigations which the act refers to as being conducted as a court. The act refers to a commissioner who shall, for the purposes of the act, be a court and who has the right to impose penalties, sanctions and the like on individuals who may be found culpable.
I submit there is an analogy to be drawn between this sort of court and a court which delves into matters between a prosecution and a defence, although it is true that this court is more of an investigation and is not exactly on all fours with a court dealing with litigation. However, the commissioner is given the powers of a court and he can impose certain penalties against individuals.
In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I think that people appearing as witnesses before

March 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
such a court should be in the same class as those appearing as witnesses in cases falling within the normal operations of our courts, such as witnesses for the prosecution or witnesses for the defence. These people are witnesses who express themselves either on one side of a case or the other and are thereby entitled to the protection that a lawyer can afford them. They are also open, of course, to the approach of the attorney for the prosecution or the defence who endeavours to break down the evidence they give, if the attorney so desires.
I think a comparable situation exists here. Individuals called as witnesses, even though, under the act as it now stands, they do not have the protection of a lawyer, should be entitled to protection, and the act should be altered to enable a person called as a witness before a formal investigation of this sort to have available to him the right to choose a lawyer to protect his rights, thus ensuring that his rights are not encroached upon.
I just press that on the minister for his consideration. Perhaps while he is making this detailed study of the Canada Shipping Act, which I am sure will be concluded during the next few months, he will include a provision along this line which will then bring the act up to date.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to rise briefly to support the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. He represents, as I do, an important shipbuilding riding in western Canada. There is no doubt that the people of British Columbia feel discriminated against in the exclusion of their ferry system, a very popular and good ferry system, from the benefits of the government's subsidy program announced in the house last January. Make no mistake about it, Mr. Chairman, the lack of a subsidy, if it persists, will result in higher costs for travelling on our ferry system.
I think I should point out to the committee and the minister that transportation is the essence of life in British Columbia. One has only to look at our mountains and islands to see we have a special problem and to realize that it means more to us probably than to any other province.
Other provinces benefit from the terms of union, Mr. Chairman, and I sometimes wish that when British Columbia entered confederation we had had a more far-seeing team 
negotiating on our behalf, in which case perhaps we too would have federally subsidized ferry operations, as do other provinces. I do not think we object to what other provinces are receiving, but we do think we should be allowed to have a fair share of federal money for this purpose.
I know that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano has asked the Minister of Transport and the Minister without Portfolio to take another look at the government's shipbuilding policy, but I would stress the urgency of taking a look now. With the completion of the ships already contracted for by the British Columbia ferry system, there is now a lack of work in our shipbuilding yards. If any future construction is held up, as I understand it will be, because of the lack of a government subsidy, then now is the time to grant a subsidy and get more ships built.
In my riding, where the yard which has just finished building the largest ferry for the B.C. ferry service is situated, some 350 men are at this moment being displaced from their work. Therefore I ask the Minister without Portfolio, if he does take another look at the policy, as I feel sure he will, to please urge his colleagues to look hard and to look now.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Halifax.

Mr. Chairman, I do not mind being referred to as the hon. member for Halifax because it so happens that I am going to say a few words of interest both to Halifax and to Saint John. We have heard a great deal this afternoon from members who have been speaking on behalf of Montreal and Vancouver. Lest my silence here on this peaceful Friday afternoon be taken to mean that am in agreement with everything they said, I want to point out that we have two national ports, Halifax and Saint John, which are just as important to this nation as Montreal and Vancouver.
The Minister without portfolio gave us a rundown on the navigational problems in the St. Lawrence waterway system, but let me tell him that one of the easiest ways he can solve those problems of navigation is to use the ports of Halifax and Saint John a little more. We have the seamen who can keep accidents to the minimum. We also have the facilities, though they may need a little attention, and we are looking for business. In this way we would avoid a lot of this discussion this afternoon and, more particularly, the spectacle af senior government members and
March 25, 1966



parliamentary secretaries trying to talk out their own supplementary estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask one question of the minister. I too listened very attentively to his remarks and I appreciate the attitude he has taken, but is it his intention when the Canada Shipping Act is rewritten to consider the establishment of a special committee of the house for this purpose? This would enable the whole act to be studied, particularly as it affects safety. Witnesses and other interested parties could be brought before the committee, with the end result of having a broad discussion of the problems facing the industry. This would enable any changes made to be complete and long lasting.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few minutes of the committee's time to express the appreciation of the Social Credit party here for the very kind words said about the Social Credit government of British Columbia and its vigorous policy of ferry construction. We did not see this as being particularly socialistic, but rather as a step that was necessary for the completion of our highways system. Perhaps if Vancouver Island had not joined with British Columbia to make one great province-and we are celebrating this as a centenary this year-but had remained isolated, there might have been a federal approach to build a causeway to link the island with the mainland. The funds for that construction have not been forthcoming. With the very vigorous highway development program the government was undertaking, it became essential for it to go into the ferry business also, to link the island with the mainland.
We have been very pleased this afternoon to hear the presentations made from the government side of the house, because those of us in this section of the house have made these presentations earlier, and we hope that we now have made some headway on this subject. Certainly, the reply of the Minister of Transport, that it would not break his heart to take a second look at ferry subsidies, is not good enough. That ought not to be allowed to stand as the last word of the government on this question. We are looking forward very eagerly to a more definite word that there will be federal participation in the subsidizing of ferry construction in British Columbia. Too much of the co-operation with the provinces in this country has tended to be

a sort of salvage operation to improve a bad situation.
I think it is time the federal government was concerned also with improving situations in provinces that are going ahead.
