Mr. Chairman, I just want to make a brief remark to the acting minister, in the minister's absence, with respect to grants which are made through his department.
We are all looking forward to the celebration of the centenary next year. A great many grants have been made through the Department of Finance to other departments, commissions and committees, which are all very commendable. I am sure that these will help to improve the centennial celebrations.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the acting minister forward to the Minister of Finance this suggestion, that the minister should consult with his colleagues in the cabinet and with representatives of the government of Ontario, with a view to recommending that a

March 25, 1966
Supply-Finance
grant be made to the city of Ottawa, so that for the centennial year when people come to visit our national capital they avoid the danger of breaking the axles of their cars when they drive down the streets in centre town. I know that this is a sensitive subject for some aldermen of the city of Ottawa. I am in full agreement with the hon. member for Skeena, in the remarks he has made on a number of occasions, to the effect that something ought to be done.
Seriously, Mr. Chairman, the streets of our national capital are a national disgrace. There are a great number of holes, both potholes and mudholes, in the streets of downtown Ottawa. We all know that the city is under a considerable handicap. It does not have industries from which it can derive taxes. We know that the government gives a grant in lieu of taxes with respect to government property. But I would ask whether, for the sake of the many thousands of people expected to come to Ottawa to celebrate the centenary, something could not be done to repair the streets in the centre of the city. It would not cost that much money; and I think nobody in Canada would disagree with me, and particularly those visiting Ottawa, who would probably appreciate this, when I say that the streets ought to be repaired.
There is another matter which is to be considered, and I do not know whether it should come under the National Research Council, or some other body of that nature. The minister could decide the details of this with his appropriate colleagues. Perhaps it could be taken up with the provincial governments of Quebec or Ontario. What I refer to, Mr. Chairman, is this: Some means should be found of removing from the air of this fair capital of ours the sort of pollution that does exist. At one time I thought it was caused by one of the large manufacturing plants in the area, The E. B. Eddy Company. I am told that one or two other companies may be involved.
I think any hon. member of this house, and indeed anybody who has ever visited Ottawa has been greeted on awakening in the morning by the sulphurous fumes that so often pollute the city. That is a national disgrace in the capital of a land that has gone to great expense advertising itself as a land of fresh air, lakes, waters, and woods. It is a disgrace that such a state of affairs should be permitted in the capital. There is no reason why this cannot be cured, and if some moneys are allocated to help alleviate some of these

problems and get rid of these noxious fumes, that will be of assistance, may I put it this way, toward the celebration of our centennial year.

Mr. Chairman, I rise at this particular juncture to make a special eleventh hour appeal to the Minister of Finance to review in his conscience once again, on this eleventh hour week end, the financial straits of hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
I submit this is the proper place for such an appeal to be made, because we are considering supplementary estimates, and because the Minister of Finance is scheduled to bring down his 1966-67 budget in this house just four days from now.
Because the new budget is so near at hand, this current week end is indeed the eleventh hour for those many thousands of Canadian families and households that are casualties of a taxation and food price juggernaut in this country that has been running wild for the past three years.
These Canadians, many of them lonely pensioners, many of them widows, many of them youthful breadwinners and housewives struggling to feed and clothe young families, have high and trusting hopes for Tuesday night. They are looking to the minister's budget that night to introduce a ray of blessed relief into their troubled economic situations.
They are looking for help to get out from under the crushing burden of prices and taxes that today saps them of their dreams, their energies and their peace of mind, and bows them under a weight as oppressive as that described by the poet's classic man with a hoe.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that for all our material affluence in Canada today, for all the sheen to our society, for all the triumphs in the realm of gross national product, there are tens of thousands of Canadian homes in 1966 in which economic survival is a continuing struggle and a continuing worry. The tightrope walk from pay day to pay day has become a way of life in Canada-the way of life, I submit, for far too many Canadian households. The Canadian householder, in far too great numbers, needs help. He needs the help of the Canadian government, and he needs the help of every man and woman in this chamber. Caught in an economic crossfire of costs and taxes, he is starting to get hit. If he is mortally wounded in that crossfire-if he
March 25, 196G

should stumble and go down-where then is the great Canadian experiment that plunges ahead today at such perilous speed? What price the glories of legislative programs which go too far, too fast? What the average Canadian is most concerned about today is the surge in the prices he meets on every hand together with the increasing bite in taxes that anywhere from two to four levels of government take out of every dollar he earns.
For my part, although I do not minimize or disparage the importance of responsible programs of social welfare, I do not believe that a country can go on ad infinitum slapping a heavier and heavier burden on the backs of its responsible, industrious citizens. They are the ones who carry the load, to be sure. They will always carry the load and, up to a reasonable point, they will do so cheerfully. But in this exercise as in many others, there comes a breaking point, and I suggest the time has come when it would be judicious and expedient for legislators in Canada to ask themselves whether they perhaps are straining the average Canadian wage earner very severely.
One cannot go on forever shifting initiative, and expect one's people, young or old, to shoot for the stars. One cannot go on forever penalizing excellence, and expect one's people, young and old, to develop Canada the way all of us wish to see her develop.
We can talk all we like about our mineral wealth and our forests and all our other fabulous natural resources. But our mightiest resources, by far outshining all others, like the north outshines the tepid tropics, are our human resources-our men and women. These are the resources we must mine. These are the crops we must harvest. We do the Canadian nation a vast and potentially fatal disservice if we blunt the ambitions of our citizens and crush their spirits, by making daily life so expensive-by making taxes so oppressive that they can never get out from under their current financial burdens, can never know freedom from worry and thus can never truly enjoy our Canadian heritage or devote their energies to participating in it creatively.
Thus I urge the minister, if he has not already done so, to provide in his budget for four measures at least: first, repeal the 11 per cent building sales tax; second, make realty taxes deductible for income tax purposes in owner-occupied homes; third, raise the basic income tax exemption level, especially for
Supp ly-Finance
widows with children to support; and, fourth, increase the old age pension along the lines this party has been asking.
Nor, I suggest, is this latter proposal necessarily inconsistent with what I have said already about the need for fitting a clamp on our soaring tax rates. I submit that no increase in taxes is necessary to support the increase we have been asking in the old age pension. The last Auditor General's report provides examples of ample sources of revenue. The annual report of the Auditor General for the year now ending, March 31, 1966, cites no less than 450 specific findings of the Glassco royal commission on government operations which were designed to eliminate wasteful practices and result in substantial savings of public funds.
In that respect I should like to quote from the following editorial in the February 10, 1966, edition of the Winnipeg Free Press. The editorial was headed "A Matter of Responsibility". With reference to these 450 recommendations, it says:
Each of these findings was followed through by the staff of the audit office to determine what action had been taken since the royal commission reported. It was found that no less than 73 per cent had not been acted upon. The most important recommendations, those which would result in the greatest savings to the treasury, remained unimplemented because of the failure of senior government officials to make the necessary decisions: "We found no lack of awareness at the various departmental levels of the need to deal with the situations. It was explained to us, however, that few changes could be made without instructions from top management."
By top management, of course, Mr. Henderson can only mean cabinet ministers, deputy ministers and heads of crown corporations who, through inertia, ignorance or sheer disinterest, have failed to take the necessary steps to implement the Glassco recommendations. The cost of their procrastination is illustrated by the fact that when the commission made its report three years ago the administrative overhead of government departments and agencies was approximately $1 billion. Today it is $1.2 billion, an increase of 20 per cent despite the implementation of about one quarter of the Glassco suggestions.
I ask: Are these not adequate and reasonable sources of revenue from which to supply the funds needed in the interests of old age pensioners to supply them with the increases which this party has been seeking. In my view the picture is clear, and the government's responsibility is clear: It is the responsibility to cope, this coming Tuesday, with the situation I have described-with the economic plight of many thousands of hard-working, constructive, valuable Canadians. Hence, my appeal at this juncture. The eleventh hour is

March 25, 1966
Supply-Finance
at hand. If the minister has not already provided for these hard pressed households in his budget to be presented on Tuesday night, I submit with all humility and respect that he still has his week end in which to do so. And I urge him with the same humility to search his heart on this point. Households all across the land are watching this situation with hope. So are hon. members on this side of the house.

I would be prepared to make my pre-budget speech, too, if I had one. But I expect to be here for the budget, so I shall wait for it.
I would ask the Minister of National Revenue to give his consideration to a matter which has been raised in letters and submissions from my own area in recent weeks. It relates to the fact that Canada intends to strike a gold coin to mark the centenary in 1967. The Minister of Finance has indicated that these coins will be included in a mint set. The request coming from many of the gold mining communities is that a single coin, the gold coin itself, be separated from the mint set so that it can be used for purposes connected with the centennial. The township of Teck in particular is interested in having a number of these coins for presentation to children in the schools, and for making other presentations. It is felt it is not too much to ask that some of these municipalities, particularly when they are so closely related to gold production, should have an opportunity of acquiring single coins for this purpose.

I can only say that I will bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance for his consideration. It would simply mean turning out more gold coins which would not be included in the sets.
I might add that some of the mining companies in my area did supply the gold used for the minting of sovereigns in 1912 and 1913. It is possible that they will be doing so again.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to participate in the discussion of the supplementary estimates of the Department of Public Works and return to a subject that I am almost convinced there is no use talking about because of the attitude of the government towards this question. I have been speaking in this house in bits and drabs, because that is the only way made available to me, about the illegal filling taking place on the north side of lake Ontario opposite the shoreline of lake Ontario as it abuts the riding of York-Humber and the riding of York West.
Before somebody starts to say that this is a local politician rising on a local question regarding an area that is only four miles long, along the waterfront, I should like to emphasize that, while I speak because of the interest of the property owners along that shoreline and because of my constituents and
March 25, 1966



the voters of West York, I am speaking primarily because of the fact that a precedent will be established here if this practice is not stopped. I have almost abandoned hope that it will be stopped, in view of the history of my representations in the matter.
Lake Ontario is "a navigable water". There have been many, many court cases that have established the fact that the St. Lawrence river and the Great Lakes system are ''navigable waters", and come under the International Boundary Waters Treaty and the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Under those headings they come within the purview of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Transport. The Minister of Public Works comes into the act by virtue of Part I of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, Revised Statutes of Canada 1952, revised in 1953, 1954 and 1956.
I first spoke on this question of illegal land filling by asking a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on March 23, 1965. At that time I asked if we could get an interpretation from the Supreme Court of Canada with regard to some of the terms used in the International Boundary Waters Treaty and the Navigable Waters Protection Act. I informed the house about three weeks ago that 11 months had gone by and I still had not received a reply from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, although the question was asked publicly in this house and recorded in Hansard. Hon. members will be interested to know that I have now received a reply from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. You will realize how hard he has studied the question, because it took him 11 months to get the reply for me.
On March 4, 1965, I asked the Minister of Justice to make a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada with regard to a word used in the International Boundary Waters Treaty which states that you cannot erect any works in international streams that would "materially" affect the level of the water on either side-that is, on the United States or Canadian side. This question was put down for discussion at ten o'clock in the evening of May 4. At that time I brought out the question regarding patented waterlots. I pointed out at that time that in the afternoon I had asked whether the government would make a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada in order to obtain a definition of the word "materially", and how this might affect 23033-203
Supply-Public Works the waters of the Great Lakes or other boundary waters.
In the evening during the ten o'clock show on May 4, 1965, as recorded at page 937 of Hansard, I added:
While I am pressing upon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) the necessity of having a definite reference to the Supreme Court for an interpretation of the word "materially", might I suggest that he also seek an interpretation of the phrase "patented waterlot"?
The phrase "patented waterlot" is a bone of contention along this four mile stretch of lake Ontario, and it will continue to bother this government until there is a definite legal interpretation of that phrase. I say it will bother the government, because we have over
4,000	miles of water along the shores of the St. Lawrence river on the Canadian side and on the Great Lakes right up to Pigeon river in this Great Lakes system. If there can be patented waterlots on the four mile stretch between the Humber river and Etobicoke creek, there can be many more waterlots throughout the entire system.
Members of parliament who are taking an intelligent interest in this matter have advised me about what they call patented waterlots on lake St. Clair, on the Detroit river and on the St. Mary river at Sault Ste. Marie. I would point out that between the Humber river and Etobicoke creek there are approximately 150 of these so-called patented water-lots lying underneath the water in that four mile stretch.
At this point I should like to pay tribute and express my appreciation to Hon. Kelso Roberts, the Minister of Lands and Forests in the provincial government Hon. John Robarts, for the several hours of time that he has given me on this subject, and for the very careful surveys that the Ontario surveyor general has prepared with regard to the waterlots in that area. I did not ask to see the patented waterlots in other areas, but in that section there are approximately 150. Hon. Kelso Roberts provided me with a detailed map showing the names of the owners and detailed histories of the lots.
This question of patented waterlots comes up in this way. Since this Liberal government came into power in April of 1963 we have had three ministers of public works, the first of which was Hon. Mr. Deschatelets, for whom I have the highest regard. Under the

March 25, 1966
Supply-Public Works Navigable Waters Protection Act it is stated specifically that:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless
(a)	the site and plans thereof have been approved by the minister; and
(b)	the work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with the plans and the regulations.
I am not a lawyer so the words appear to be perfectly plain to me. If one is a lawyer he becomes filled up with the belief that everything is indistinct, hazy and fuzzy, and that one cannot assume a word means what it is supposed to mean. Otherwise lawyers would not get their fees, if they did not get into court and fight with one another about the interpretation of words.
On May 4, 1965 when I asked the then minister of justice about the word "materially", and the phrase "patented waterlot" the then parliamentary secretary to the minister of justice, Mr. Donald Macdonald, the hon. member for Rosedale came to the late show and read this statement:
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recognize at once that this is an important and very serious question in respect of which the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) and the hon. member for York West (Mr. Kelly) have been very active. X think it is very clear from the presentation this evening by the hon. member for York-Humber that both as a matter of fact and as a matter of law this is an exceedingly complicated question. It is a very difficult situation which involves an interpretation of a federal statute, the Navigable Waters Protection Act, as well as an interpretation of the Boundary Waters Treaty. This will involve very difficult questions of law. The Department of Justice will want to give serious consideration to both the suggestions of the hon. member, that binding interpretations of the relevant provisions be sought from the appropriate authorities.
That was May 4, 1965, approximately 11 months ago. At that time he was disturbed about an application from some real estate developers in the city of Montreal who were anxious to build a bridge from the north side of the St. Lawrence to the Island of Ste Therese, which is in the riding of Mercier represented by my good friend Prosper Boulanger. Mr. Deschatelets, then the Minister of Public Works,

realized that "no work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site and plans thereof have been approved by the Minister; and the work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with the plans and the regulations."
Mr. Deschatelets spent a great deal of time worrying about this application because I believe he thought that, being a member with a Montreal seat, if he granted permission somebody would say he was showing favouritism to the municipality from which he came. But we on the committee said to him, "This is a matter that can be decided, as to whether or not this is interfering with navigation and whether or not the plans have been filed in advance with you and approved by the engineers of the department." After some weeks of discussion, during which time people came up from Montreal and objected to the bridge being built on the ground that it world interfere with their activity in sailing dinghies around the island, it was decided that because the number of people interested in establishing homes on the island of Ste. Therese was greater than those who might be inconvenienced in their sailing activities, and since it did not interfere with navigation as generally understood, permission should be granted.
Mr. Deschatelets granted a permit for the construction of this bridge over the St. Lawrence between the north shore and the Island of Ste Therese. Interestingly enough, while the permit has been granted, no bridge has been built as yet. But I will come back to that.
I hold in my hand the plans that were submitted by the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission to the Department of Public Works. Surely to heavens they are a big enough outfit to know what they are doing. I am an Ontario resident and taxpayer, and I know how many lawyers the Ontario Hydro have in their employ. It was their desire in 1958 to erect a coal unloading dock in lake Ontario at Lakeview, Ontario, just about half a mile west of Etobicoke creek in the riding of Peel. This coal unloading dock is a vast structure extending out into the lake some distance so that coal boats can come in and unload on to the mechanical conveyors of the great plant at Lakeview owned by the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission. This coal is used to build up steam so that the plant is able to function 24 hours a day.
March 25, 1966

If this is such a great question of law and everybody on earth has to ask, "What does it mean?", why did the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission ask the Department of Public Works for permission to erect the wharf? The application was made in May, 1958 and was accompanied, as the law requires, by detailed plans and blueprints. I have here the approval of the application granted on August 20, 1958, and signed by H. A. Young, deputy minister of public works. There is nothing in here about this being a great, hazy question. Everybody knew exactly what they were doing and they did it properly. As a result we have a fine generating plant in Lakeview.
I hold in my hand an application by the municipality of Metropolitan Toronto. This application was filed on August 16, 1963, and is addressed to the chief of legal services, Department of Public Works, Ottawa, Ontario. The application had plans attached to it. It was to build a bridge from Olympic Island to Centre Island in Toronto harbour. This bridge is a small archway with about 16 feet clearance from the water. When this application came forward Hon. Mr. Des-chatelets was again quite disturbed because he was concerned over the words of the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
The committee met with him in his office on more than one occasion. People came down from Toronto who operated small pleasure boats, and they maintained that they put their boats at anchor every night between Olympic Island and Centre Island and felt that the bridge should not be erected. But after full and due consideration Mr. Des-chatelets, as Minister of Public Works, granted the municipality of Metropolitan Toronto the right to build this bridge from Olympic Island to Centre Island with a clearance of 16 feet above the normal water line. The application was dated August 16, 1963, and the permit was granted on August 17, 1964.
In connection with this application nobody said they did not know what the law was, or what it should be, or how it should be done, or asked whether they were going to consult the privy council in Great Britain or the high court of France. They just followed the law as it is set out in the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
I also have in my hand a letter from the Toronto Harbour Commissioners. They are a smart organization of able men. The general manager is a lawyer, but in addition they have legal counsel. They wanted to build what you or I might call a spit of land or a 23033-2031
Supply-Public Works spit of rock to the east of Toronto Island, down near Cherry street, so that they could extend the size and scope of Toronto harbour. They knew about the Navigable Waters Protection Act which says that "no work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site and plans thereof have been approved by the minister". So the Toronto Harbour Commissioners, understanding English when they see it and not realizing what a terrifically difficult problem this was, filed an application with the Department of Public Works for a filling operation and the construction of two headlands on the shoreline of Lake Ontario between Cherry and Leslie streets, Toronto, province of Ontario.
The application came in on December 29,
1964,	and was granted under date June 8,
1965,	after five months consideration. The Toronto Harbour Commissioners are not the type of people who will proceed unless the law is clear. If they do not know what the law is, they do not proceed. I have given the examples of the real estate developers in Montreal, the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission, the municipality of Metropolitan Toronto and the Toronto Harbour Commissioners, all of whom followed the letter of the law, submitted plans in advance, had them approved and then went ahead and lived up to the plans as submitted and approved.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
What have we got in the ridings of West York and York-Humber? We have people there dumping thousands of tons of fill along the shoreline of Lake Ontario in order to extend the length of their property out into the lake, without submitting any proper plans to the Department of Public Works, without asking for consent, and simply getting it ready for real estate development. In the township of Etobicoke, in that portion of it which is in my riding, private developers have gone to a point where over the years they have thrown thousands of tons of fill into lake Ontario. Now, they have gone before the Ontario Municipal Board and have had the area zoned for apartment house buildings, for motels and for restaurants. This is made land that has never been approved by the federal Department of Public Works.
When I have spoken in the past about Millgate Park development off Long Branch, people seemed to rush to the conclusion that there was only one case in point. I have said before, and I can only repeat, that I am using

March 25, 1966
Supply-Public Works Millgate as an example. I could give you another 20 cases by measurement and location if you wanted. I give you Millgate because it is the clearest example at the moment. There are about 20 similar cases in that four-mile stretch. Millgate have a lawyer, Mr. James F. McCallum, whose clients simply went to work and threw in earth obtained from the building of the subway in the city of Toronto to build up this piece of property. The property now extends 450 feet into the lake, is 330 feet in width and stands eight to ten feet above the water level of Lake Ontario.
The Millgate people have based their action in dropping this fill into Lake Ontario without the prior consent of the Department of Public Works on the ground that they own the waterlots. They are, therefore, they claim able to fill them in, as they very much wish to do as owners. As I have said in this house before, and as I repeat, we in the area have communicated with the ablest lawyers in the country. One of them in particular, in whom I have 100 per cent unbounded confidence, has told us that waterlots should not be filled, that this is an interference with navigation. He points out that the bed of the lake belongs to the province of Ontario and they can sell it to whom they wish. Once you have acquired a waterlot, you are the owner but you are only allowed to build on it such appurtenances as are required for the handling of ships which you may wish to tie up for the night.
The waterlot idea developed 100 years ago when people had boats and when, instead of beaching them each night, because of the weight which would require great strength or some mechanical means to pull them in, people began to buy waterlots to tie up these boats. Having informed the government that they wished to anchor a boat, they were not allowed to obstruct other boats crossing the waterlots.
Now, when I raise the point that this Millgate land development is being filled in, and filled in without any prior consent from the Department of Public Works, I have to emphasize that I am talking about private property. These public bodies such as the Toronto Harbour Commission, the Ontario Hydro Commission and the municipality of metropolitan Toronto are public bodies and the federal government grants them the permission they seek because it is in the public good. Why are the private owners of water-lots allowed to get away with a false claim

that they own the waterlots and therefore can fill them in, whether or not they constitute a detriment to navigation.
I have raised this question of the Navigable Waters Protection Act many times in connection with this Millgate development. I have raised it times without number in the moment or two you are allowed for a question, or during the seven minutes you are allowed on the late show. Hon. members may say that I spoke on this matter during the interim supply debate on February 10, which is not too long ago. I want to say to you that I spoke at length at that time. If you want a perfect example of how much attention this cabinet pays to a private member who raises a matter, then I refer you to a letter sent to the Millgate development people and dated March 3.
I have mentioned this matter time after time. On February 10 I spoke at some length and asked the Department of Public Works not to grant approval of the application for a retaining wall around this illegal fill because I maintain, and I think quite properly, that this illegal addition should be nationalized by the crown. It could be turned into a public park for the people of the area. This would also kill a precedent that is now being built up to the effect that if you have a waterlot you can do what you like with it.
I spoke on February 10, 1966 and I just want hon. members to know the attention the cabinet pays to anybody objecting to private desires-or perhaps they are only subject to the blandishments of friends other than me. Under date of March 3, the department wrote as follows:
Re: Application for approval of a proposed retaining wall (around fill) (In Lake Ontario in front of Lot 9, broken front con., Township of Etobicoke, County of York), Province of Ontario.
Dear Sir:
I acknowledge receipt of proof of publication of the necessary advertising relating to the above application.
Approval of this application Is being delayed pending full investigation and report of complaints received against approval of the sea wall.
Yours very truly,
Peter Sorokan,
Chief of Legal Services.
Now, this letter must have filled Millgate Park investment people with a great deal of pleasure because it says that "approval" of this application is being delayed. They could not use a phrase such as, "Consideration will be given to this application during the next few weeks". No, these private developers,
March 25, 1966

evidently with an approach to the government not generally known to the public, are told, despite all the times we have drawn attention to it, that "approval of this application" is being delayed pending full investigation and report of complaints received against approval of the sea wall.
Under date of October 22, 1965, the Department of Public Works wrote to Millgate Park Investments Limited, 2788 Bathurst Street, as follows:
Dear Sir:
Our engineers now report that the plans and description which accompanied your application are considered satisfactory. It will be in order for you, therefore, to proceed with publication of the necessary advertising in the Canada Gazette and two local newspapers, and submit proof thereof upon completion on the form attached hereto.
This was two or three weeks before the general election on November 8, and there was no publicity given to that letter in the riding of West York or in the riding of York-Humber, I can assure you. This letter is signed, Peter Sorokan, Chief of Legal Services. The point I am desirous of making is this: Why is it that public bodies fill in applications in advance, accompanied by the necessary plans and the necessary advertising, but private developers are allowed to get away with whatever they want to do. They can throw tons and tons of fill into the lake. Is it because of the lawyers they hire? Is it because of the people they know, or what? Why are private developers allowed to fill in Lake Ontario? I don't get the idea. You can still buy lots from the government I believe. There were 150 private, patented waterlots along that shore.
It is the Ontario government that has sold the private waterlots. Who is to stop the Ontario government from selling more of these lots. Once they have sold the lots, is a precedent now being established that private developers can fill in the waterlots and get a screwball answer from the Department of Public Works that there is no substantia] interference with commercial navigation. The law does not read that way, it says "interfere with navigation". The present Minister of Justice who was formerly Minister of Public Works, made the announcement that Millgate Park did not interfere with navigation at all. This was quite an answer, and was given to us on February 1, 1966.
Of course, there is no obstruction to navigation created by this 450 foot spit of land on which they are hoping to build two 18 storey apartment houses. Anybody can understand
Supply-Public Works
that when you have a piece of land projecting 450 feet into Lake Ontario, with water on three sides of it and two 18 storey apartments going to be erected on it, this constitutes no obstruction to navigation. I never heard of such an answer.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I do not believe the government even knew about the plans. The Navigable Waters Protection Act says you cannot interfere with navigation. It does not refer to commercial navigation, which was another answer we got on June 1, 1965. The Department of Public Works announced that this was no interference with commercial navigation. But the act says "with navigation" and does not have the adjective "commercial" in the text.
I do not know what action we can take to nationalize this land. I have asked the government time and again on different occasions, and I ask them once more, whether they will make a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada to ascertain what are the legal rights of owners of patented waterlots. These patented water lots do not give the owner the right to fill them in with earth without the prior consent of the Department of Public Works; and I doubt whether the Department of Public Works would approve the application of a private individual made on behalf of a private citizen.
I would ask the government once more whether they will make a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada to clarify this matter, and whether they will delay the approval they seem determined to give to this applicant until such time as a decision has been handed down in the matter by the Supreme Court of Canada.

AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION FROM QUEBEC
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-10, to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1965, with respect to representation of the provinces in the Senate and qualifications of Senators.
He said:

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-10 is to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1965, with respect to representation of the provinces in the Senate and qualifications of senators.
This bill mainly suggests amendments to sections 22 and 23, as well as the repeal of sections 26, 27 and 28 of the present act.
Mr. Speaker, section 23 reads as follows:
The qualification of a senator shall be as follows:
(1)	He shall be of the full age of thirty years;
(2)	He shall be either a natural-born subject of the queen, or a subject of the queen naturalized by an act of the parliament of Great Britain, or of the parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, or of the legislature of one of the provinces of Upper Canada, Lower Canada, Canada, Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick, before the Union, or of the parliament of Canada, after the Union;
[The Chairman.]
The purpose of Bill C-10 is simply to give a more Canadian character to those sections of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1965, to repeal section 23 and substitute the following therefor:
The qualification of a senator shall be as follows:
(1)	He shall be of the full age of thirty years:
(2)	He shall be a Canadian citizen:
(3)	He shall be resident In the province for which he is appointed.
Now, if we consider section 22 of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1965, we find that paragraph (6) section 23, the repeal of which is also being proposed, was inserted in our constitutional act at the time of confederation to protect the English speaking Protestant minority, mainly grouped in the eastern townships of Quebec at the time. Of course, no such provision was made to protect the French speaking Catholic minorities in the other provinces.
It seems to me that, at this time, when bilingualism and respect for the founding races, not only of one province but of Canada as a whole, are in the fore it is time the provisions of the British North America Acts (1867 to 1965) be amended and adapted to 1966, to the time in which we are living.
Mr. Speaker, if we look at the representation of every province, in the Senate, we find that Ontario, which is entitled to 24 senators, has only two French speaking members. For the province of Quebec, four Senators are English speaking, compared with 20 French speaking for a total of 24.
For Nova Scotia, not one French speaking senator among the ten.
For New Brunswick, three out of ten senators are French speaking; for Prince Edward Island, none out of four; for British Columbia, none out of six; for Manitoba, one out of six, for Saskatchewan, one out of six; for Alberta, none out of six, and for Newfoundland, none out of six.
Mr. Speaker, a senator for Alberta died recently, Senator Aristide Blais.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Then, pressure was brought to bear by various Alberta associations.
I have here a letter from the president of the French Canadian Association of Alberta, which says:
Dear Sir:
You will readily appreciate how disappointed the Franco-Albertans were when they learned that hon. Senator Aristide Blais' successor was not a French Canadian. We find it difficult to understand this decision taken by the Prime Minister of Canada
March 25, 1966

and we hope that he will correct this omission at the earliest opportunity.
We presume that you share our views on this matter and that, in due course, you will make the proper representations.
You will find enclosed copy of a resolution which was passed by the members of the general council of the French Canadian Association of Alberta and which was sent to the Rt. Hon. Lester B. Pearson on March 7, 1966.
We expect that, in the not too distant future, a few vacancies will occur in the representation of Alberta in the Senate and we deem it most advisable to continue asking what we began to ask immediately after Senator Blais' death, in November 1964. We are counting on your support and we thank you in advance.
Mr. Speaker, this stand taken by the French Canadian Association of Alberta should surprise no one in this house.
In the province of Quebec, we have always accepted that English speaking senators be appointed to a seat in the Senate to represent the Protestant Anglo Saxon minority of our province. The province of Quebec never raised any objection whatsoever about the representation which is quite normal and respectable and which we respect.
I make it four provinces out of ten which do not have a single French speaking representative in the Canadian Senate, and that seems quite illogical to me.
We suggest that this lack of logic be remedied and that is why I introduce Bill No. C-10 which asks that senators be Canadian citizens.
I will add, in passing, that the bicultural character of our country must be taken into account, not only in one region but throughout the country, in all the provinces; what we accept in the province of Quebec should be done in the other provinces.
It was rather surprising, in the circumstances, to see appointments such as the ones which were made quite recently and for which the Prime Minister of Canada did not take that fact into account.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Prime Minister, who likes to champion the rights of the two ethnic groups which founded Canada, should take that fact into account, not only when he makes a speech in the house but when he makes appointments.
Mr. Speaker, the proposed change is motivated mainly by the fact that Canada is no longer a colony, and therefore only Canadians should be eligible for the Senate.
You know that, under the present act, a senator can be appointed from Great Britain, Australia or any commonwealth nation.
British North America Act
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, only Canadians should be eligible for the Senate because we live in a country which is now sovereign.
Let us add also that, if it is most difficult for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven, a poor man should not be prevented from entering the democratic Senate of the kingdom of Canada.
Paragraph 6 is deleted for the reasons given in the explanatory note opposite Section 1.
With regard to Sections 26, 27 and 28 of the said act, no use has ever been made of these sections since confederation, that is 1867. They are therefore antiquated, useless, and I suggest we simply delete them, so that they might not cause inconvenience to anyone at a later date, especially from 1966 on.
In Section 4, I request that this act be cited as the
British North America Act, 1966 and the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1965 and this Act may be cited together as the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1966.
Mr. Speaker, I believe this bill is prejudicial to no one. On the contrary, it confirms the fact that ours is a sovereign nation; its purpose is to establish clearly that to become a senator, one must be 30 years of age, a Canadian citizen and a resident in the province for which one is appointed.
That is the purpose of the bill and I trust that the house as well as the members are wise enough to understand the importance of proving to Canada that our country is sovereign and that we can act, in all consciousness, and freely, in favour of Canada, with Canadians.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION FROM QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this is the first time I have the honour to participate in the discussion in this house, I hope my colleagues will grant me the privilege of giving my speech to the end.
I am particularly fortunate to speak on a much discussed subject of major significance. In the past, many members have seen fit to rise to move amendments concerning the honourable members of the senate.
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a bill introduced by the hon. member for Vil-leneuve (Mr. Caouette) who thinks it is proper to suggest also changes which directly affect our colleagues of the upper house.
I am very proud to follow my hon. friend because I have high regard for his oratory,
March 25, 1966

British North America Act for his devotion to his work, for his fighting spirit and for his perseverance.
I sincerely believe that the whole of our population deserves to be well informed on the important role played by the members of the Canadian senate.
But since this is my maiden speech, I also want to say that I will respect the rule of progression, to wit that one must walk before one can run, but while making steady progress in accordance with the policies laid down by my Liberal colleagues. Philosophy states that nature does not leap. Nevertheless, I intend to follow my own course of action resulting from sustained toil.
I also wish to add, Mr. Speaker, that I intend, together with my French and English speaking colleagues in the house, to remain objective in my remarks and my discussions. I also would express the hope that we may experience Canadian unity to its full extent.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I also want to say that, if I intend to work in close co-operation with one and all, it is because this is my way of proclaiming proudly that I wish to be among those who will say, with dignity and enthusiasm, that French speaking Canadians certainly intend to co-operate, but they also want their rights to be respected. I want to be among those who will be able to say: French Canadians no longer intend to symbolize the sheep, but the Precursor.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to make a review of that place we call the upper chamber. Naturally, Massieu said: gratitude is the heart's memory. That is why, with the permission of the house, I should like to assess properly the part played by the hon. members of the Senate.
Mr. Speaker, our upper house is now made up of 102 members appointed by the governor general under the great seal of Canada.
It is in order to mention here that the act contains a special provision under which four or eight additional senators can be appointed to represent the four great regions of Canada. However, as far as I know, that provision has never been used since confederation.
Considering that, in the last several years, the number of our members has increased and that our population keeps increasing and that its needs should be better met, and that some regions are not represented, I ask, Mr. Speaker, that the provisions of the act be applied and that the Northwest Territories
[Mr. Neveu.l
for instance have a member in the upper house because all Canadians, whether English or French speaking, whether they belong to one ethnic group or other, deserve to be represented not only in this House of Commons but also in the upper house, so that all Canadians are represented.
According to constitutional tradition, the Prime Minister has the power to appoint senators by sending a recommendation to the governor general who accepts it.
I would hope however that in the future it might be possible to suggest an amendment to the effect that the Prime Minister, in agreement with the members of the Privy Council, could recommend the appointment of senators, to avoid any purely political discussion or nomination, and to enable all Canadians who built our economy in all sectors, whether they are in politics or not, to represent us permanently in the upper chamber.
As you know, Senate representation is the following in Canada: Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes each have 24 senators; Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, 10 each; Prince Edward Island, four; Newfoundland, six; and western Canada, 24, each of the four western provinces being represented by six senators.
In the case of each division of Canada, excluding the province of Quebec, senators are named without any designation of constituency, that is to say they represent the whole of the region for which they are appointed.
As far as Quebec is concerned, one senator is provided for each of the 24 electoral colleges of the territory which made up the old Lower Canada. Personally, I favour maintaining that particular system because it better identifies our province which was one of the two pioneers and, therefore, proves clearly its role as one of the founding nations.
That formula is fair and most praiseworthy because it enables our various regions to depend on one representative who keeps constantly in mind the problems which concern more particularly the constituency he represents.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is appropriate to review the qualifications of a member of the upper house.
As was said earlier, one must be over 30 years old and be a British subject. On that last point, I feel that, because of the amendments which gave our country its independence, qualification should be changed from British subject to Canadian subject. That
March 25, 1966	COMMONS
provision would help to a certain extent to recognize an adult Canada, therefore more modern, considering the powers put at our disposal.
One must also own, in the province for which one is appointed, real estate of a minimum value of $4,000 over and above debts and liabilities, and real and personal property of a minimum value of $4,000 also over and above debts and liabilities. In the case of Quebec, one must reside in the province or own real estate valued at $4,000 in the riding for which one is appointed.
The Senate was never meant to compete with the House of Commons in the field of legislation. It was created as a second house and as Sir John A. Macdonald said, it can give "sober second thought" to bills introduced in the house. That has been, generally, its role.
By virtue of the constitution, financial bills, that is bills which entail any expenditure of public funds or which levy taxes, must first be introduced in the House of Commons, as is done in the United Kingdom.
In every other respect, the Senate is the equal of the House of Commons, as the two must agree in the enactment of any legislative measure.
Finally, the Senate has an absolute right of veto over all bills, a right it has exercised from time to time. It has also claimed, and in fact exercised, the right to amend money bills when such amendments decreased the amounts involved, or the taxes levied, and did not increase the burden placed upon the taxpayers.
Confederation had barely been signed when clamours for Senate reform started and continued periodically. On several occasions it was the target of severe criticism, often of a contradictory nature. It was accused of not being responsible to the people of being a possible menace to the supremacy of the House of Commons, of being a mere rubber stamp for the House of Commons, of comprising too great a number of representatives of one political party or the other, of not bearing its rightful share of the legislative burden.
Moreover, it has been said on various occasions that an age limit should be set for senators. An amendment was passed and enacted to this effect on June 2, 1965 and it now appears in Chapter 4 of the Statutes of Canada 14, Elizabeth II, under the title: An Act to make provision for the retirement of
DEBATES	3223
British North America Act members of the Senate. Under this amendment, the age of retirement of senators appointed after this date has been set at 75.
Nevertheless, many factors were against any appreciable change in the composition, the method of appointment and operation of the Senate.
First of all, there has been a tendency to expect too much of that institution. Numerous critics were based on a misconception of the proper duties of the Senate, as mentioned previously. The role of the Senate was never to compete with the house of commons nor, as Sir Robert Borden said "to make use of its powers to the limit of the law." Thus, it never opposed passage of a bill for which the government had received a mandate from the people at a general election.
Traditionally, the Senate has always been conscious of the special role it has to play in the enacting of legislation, and of the fact that it must check but not obstruct measures sent to it by the house of commons. Indeed, no attempt has been made until now to restrict its powers although, under the Imperial Parliament Act, the powers of the house of lords, the equivalent of the Senate in the United Kingdom, have been considerably curtailed.
Second, let us note that public opinion has never reached a consensus as to the means of reforming the Senate, as previously mentioned; there are many conflicting possibilities in this regard, and the views of the government, and those of the opposition differed, understandably, with regard to both the urgency of reform and the points which should be subjected to reform. These differences depended on whether or not the majority in the Senate was of the same political stripe as the government.
Third, political parties in this country seem to agree on the fact that the basic provisions of the British North America Act in regard to the composition, the method of appointment and the duties of the Senate cannot be amended, without prior consultation with the provincial governments, although, in strict accordance with the law, parliament could probably take several steps on its own under the 1949 constitutional amendment previously referred to in my remarks.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Finally, let us not forget any proposed reform requiring the intervention of the
March 25. 1966

British North America Act Canadian parliament must be approved by the Senate itself.
In spite of periodical reform proposals, no one should be under the impression that the Senate has nothing to do in the making of our laws. However, in the red chamber there is neither the animation of the Commons, nor the climate of political rivalry which prevails here. Debates are sober, speeches are short and concise. As an outstanding parliamentarian once said: "It is a workshop, not a theatre".
In the Senate, discussions which are purely political in character, procedural disputes and filibustering are held at a minimum. Legislation is put forward and debated usually in a calm atmosphere. During parliamentary sessions, therefore, the Senate meets less often than the house, and its sittings are shorter than those of the house where, as can be seen constantly, there is always a current, or at least a strong undercurrent of political emulation, because members must always look after their own chances of re-election and that of their party.
In fact, the Senate performs carefully and efficiently, mainly through its committees, a great deal of parliamentary work without being given much credit for it and without getting much publicity.
Sponsors of bills have to prove their case before the appropriate Senate committee, and a private bill passed by the Senate is very seldom significantly or repeatedly amended by the House of Commons. Finally, the Senate discusses and considers regularly various matters of public interest and reports to the house. In this connection, the wishes of the Senate are often reflected ultimately in government legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the distinguished members of that house are really objective; most of them have a wide experience in the judicial, political and social fields, as well as in the business world. Many of them have an extensive knowledge and have distinguished themselves in this house. They are quite familiar with our statutes and understand thoroughly the proper functioning of our society.
In the past few years, the numerous general elections have brought about radical changes in the representation within the House of Commons. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the human element has always played a major role in human relationships.

The members of the Senate are permanent members of parliament who, the year round, work in teams and study dispassionately the bills presented to them.
This parliamentary stability makes for solid friendships based on the recognition of others. These men ceaselessly learn to respect one another because they know how to respect.
Mr. Speaker, during the critical times we are living through, our distinguished members of the Senate are playing a magnificent role in enabling our two founding races, our two languages, our two cultures, to be accepted everywhere in our beautiful country.
The members of the upper house can set for the people of Canada an example that unity must necessarily be prectised through constructive dialogue so that there may be a real possibility of solving the many problems that occur in our time.
Representing all the provinces of Canada, our honourable colleagues may from the same starting point, disseminate the message of unity to which all right-minded citizens of Canada sincerely aspire.
The example of the members of the upper house must be followed and I express the hope, Mr. Speaker, that all my colleagues maintain such objectivity. Our soldiers, whether French or English speaking, laboured together for a common goal and many of them spilled their blood to preserve our freedom; they did so in order that all Canadians labour together in peace, to build a new Canada that will set forth, all sails to the wind, toward continued progress.
Mr. Speaker, the members of the Senate make up a huge laboratory from which came out the experience and the means to help us strengthen the ties which will serve as an example for all Canadians. And before concluding my remarks, I would like to quote two great men. In 1959, Dr. Schweitzer said:
One must never hurl unfounded rumors against an opponent or impute motives to him because he, like anyone else, is inhabited by the spirit.
In closing, I would like to strike a note of friendly unity by quoting from Saint-Exupery's book Terre des Hommes:
To love is not to look at each other but to look together in the same direction.

Mr. Speaker, when I was asked whether I would take part in this debate I gave some period of study to this bill, and I found some things which I do not think I knew about previously concerning Canada's constitution and about the Senate. What I found, something which I thought was most interesting, is that at the time of confederation Quebec was the only province entering confederation which had a singular arrangement in respect of the appointment of senators. In that province, as has been explained well in the bill presented by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), they appointed their senators on a geographic basis, based on the irregular boundaries or counties of the old province of Lower Canada. However, my friend says this was done with a view to providing an adjustment between the English and the French population of that day, and it did indeed have a considerable amount to do with the fact that the eastern townships at that time were more heavily populated with English speaking persons than they are today.
To go to some of the texts which describe this, I think it would be of interest to hon. members if I quoted a few remarks from some authorities on this subject, to shed a little more light on why this was done and exactly how it was done. I refer to a book by Robert A. MacKay, entitled "The Unreformed Senate of Canada", in which he says:
The basis of representation in the upper house was the great compromise of the conference, just as it had been in the convention of the American States at Philadelphia. At Philadelphia the compromise was equal representation in the upper house for the states, at Quebec it was equal representation for the three sections.
DEBATES	3225

That is to say, the country was divided into three sections; the mari times with 24 senatorial seats, Quebec or French Canada with 24 senatorial seats and Upper Canada, which at that time had not expanded westward, with 24 senatorial seats.
He then says:
It was the key to federation, 'the very essence of the compact,' said George Brown. 'Our Lower Canadian friends have agreed to give us representation by population in the Lower House, on the express condition that they could have equality in the Upper House. On no other condition could we have advanced a step.'
That is another question which the hon. member takes up in his bill. That is, the question of property ownership as being a requisite in order to qualify for a senatorship.
Mr. MacKay then states:
This provision, which was of concern only to Canada, seems to have been worked out among members of the government representing Lower Canada. Its purpose was to assure to both the French speaking Roman Catholic majority and the English speaking Protestant minority their fair share of representation in the upper house. It applied and still applies, only to Quebec.
Let us now turn to the confederation debates, and I am sure all hon. members have a copy of them in their own libraries. We find at page 236 the words of the hon. Sir E. P. Tache who said in 1865:
Perhaps it is well that we have now responsible government, because responsible government is a cure for many evils. Well, the bill to give Protestant dissenters-
Perhaps my hon. friend will be interested in that phrase. The English were referred to as "Protestant dissenters" in Lower Canada.
Sir E. P. Tache continues:
Well, the bill to give Protestant dissenters in Lower Canada certain rights was opposed again and again in the Legislative Council of Lower Canada, and opposed by English Protestants. But this was no less a proof of the liberality of the French Canadians.
At this point in brackets are the words "hear, hear". That is one of the things we miss in our Hansard today, these little interjections which tell us when there was laughter and applause in the house.

I will not continue to read his words, but he does go on to say how he had taken part in setting up this peculiar difference in the selection of senators from Quebec, on the county basis rather than on a regional basis as was the case in the rest of the country.
I am a little surprised that my hon. friend would want to give up the territorial distribution of senatorships in the province of Quebec even though, as he said, the English element has to a considerable extent now left the eastern townships. Do the geographic districts for the distribution of senatorships not protect the French speaking citizens of Quebec? If they were not there, would it not be possible, for example, for a prime minister to appoint all his senators from the area of Montreal or, indeed from the city of West-mount? Under the system as it now is the senators of Quebec, more so than in any other province or area of Canada, must indeed be appointed from a specific area and must give representation to a geographic area of that province.
While I am referring to this subject, I should like to skip a little bit in the member's bill and point out to the fact that an individual, in order to qualify for a senatorship, must also possess property. It was part of the constitution at confederation that at the same time geographic distribution of senatorships in the province of Quebec was established, the appointees had also to possess property in the districts they were to represent.
In my province of British Columbia we divide up the senatorial appointments among the island, the lower mainland or metropolitan area and the interior of the province. I do not think this is done on any constitutional basis, but simply as a long-standing practice in distributing the six senatorships to which the province of British Columbia is now entitled.
The difficulty in this regard is this. As soon as we go to the interior and appoint a senator he moves from the area into the city and we seldom see him back in the interior again. If he sells his property he disappears almost entirely from that area and cannot, therefore, give the kind of representation to the area that he might otherwise give if he were constrained to keep property in that area as the senator representing the geographic location.

Far from being a hindrance or something that a person would want to rid himself of in a bill of this kind, I would think the hon. member would want to retain this requirement in the bill in order to encourage senators not to give up their farms and move into flats here in Ottawa, seldom going back to the communities from which they had been sent as representatives in the Senate. It seems to me this would be a very desirable feature and one which we might wish had been included in the arrangements at the time of confederation for other provinces as well as Quebec.
I now want to turn for a moment to the subject of Canadian citizenship, because this is one subject about which I heard the hon. gentleman speak. I know a little bit about his views regarding Canadian citizenship and, indeed, a bit about his views regarding French and English speaking Canadians. But, of course, there has always been a great struggle in Canada in the making of appointments to the Senate, because there is always an attempt to make them not only on geographic lines, as set out for us by the constitution, but on ethnic, religious and class lines. In that regard I mean classes such as individuals who come from the country, from the city and from labouring sections of the community as well as those from managerial and professional sections. All those considerations must be looked into when the Prime Minister comes to the permutations involved in choosing Senate appointments.

He goes on to say at page 51:
The French Canadians of Ontario and western Canada seem to attach the same kind of political-social-psychological significance to representation in the Senate. When J. H. G. Lacasse from Ontario was summoned to the Upper House in 1928, Cas-grain made a special point during the Address debate in the House of Commons: "I am pleased to observe," he said, "that the government has fulfilled a duty: they have acknowledged the rights of the French Canadian minority in Ontario, by calling to the Upper House one of its distinguished citizens-and I think all the French Canadian people of the province of Quebec, as well as those of other parts of Canada, will give credit to the government-for such a fair and just act."
A little further on he says:
Claims of this nature are of course not restricted to the major minority groups. Indeed, there are nearly as many claims to representation in the Senate as there are minorities of whatever complexion. Thus, for example, the Hebrew Conservative Political Association, Montreal, said in its resolution, June 28, 1926, that, "Whereas from a national and political point of view the time has arrived when it would be highly desirable that the Conservative party should give due prominence and recognition to a member of the Jewish race by an appointment to the Senate of Canada ...be it resolved that we...hereby unanimously recommend the appointment of Isaac Lande to the Senate of Canada."
Then the writer of this book says:
Again, when Mr. J. Hnatyshyn was summoned to the Senate in 1959, the Saskatoon Star Phoenix commented: "The appointment of Mr. John Hnatyshyn, Q.C., as a Senator of Canada is a meritorious one and is so acclaimed in Saskatoon and beyond, and regardless of party affiliations and party considerations-the underlying importance of this appointment to the Red Chamber is in the fact that Mr. Hnatyshyn is a native of the Ukraine, and his choice-as the first of his race in Saskatchewan to go to the Senate is a recognition of the great role Canadian Ukrainians have played, and are continuing to play in this growing country."
So it is that prime ministers in the past have attempted in their choice of Senators to give recognition to walks of life in Canada and representation to the wide diversification of ethnic groups which have made up this great country. They have even gone outside the boundaries of Quebec to select senators and give representation to French Canadian minorities outside that province, just as my hon. friend has asked this house to provide by way of constitutional amendment.
In his remarks the hon. member for Vil-ieneuve said there had not been, for example, a French Canadian appointment from the province of British Columbia. I should like to remind him that the late Senator Turgeon,
